paragraphs.text: [1.] [?] … but no less than is fitting. [?] small matters were able to [?] such strength, and in my mind to meet, not unnaturally, the love that perfects your modesty. Even if it is mixed with another kind of wisdom, the kind acquired from the business of affairs, still, at once and in it, as in the very goodness of your perfect love, I shall be greatly delighted, when in due time the fruits of exactness [?] are repaid after trial with the many drops of God's goodness, and the gloom of the winter air of afflictions turns to the clear sky of spring, and the light of deliverance dawns on us from the great Sun of Righteousness. Then our mouth will be filled with laughter and our tongue with praise. Then they will say among the nations, "The Lord has done great things for these," and we too will say boldly, "The Lord has done great things for us, and we are glad." To him be glory for ever. Amen. Why then, O wise one, [do you think it fitting] to ask after the welfare of those you love like a servant, in a few lines on paper? For it seems you would not even be pleased if they wrote to you. For I have once and for all become the servant of the love of your honour, and I count it an excellent thing for keeping your memory through such a commerce of letters. So I have now resolved to come and meet your face, and I do not suppose that you will reject the eagerness of my mind.

So if you want to meet these things gladly, do not withhold the good gift of your thoughts from those who are waiting to hear of your health. Greet the sharers [?] of your labours. All the holy ones here, who do not cease to pray for us at the offering of the holy mysteries, ask after your welfare. May God fulfil this through their prayers, as befits the mercies of his goodness. Amen.
2. To the community of monks, concerning zeal for the faith.

To the father holy in all things, the blessed Mar Babai, your son Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. O father, if the practice of good were glorified in every generation with fitting glory, [?] even those who struggle with feeble strength in the contest of battles would have the world [?] before them. That praise, coming from many, would add strength to the weakness of their zeal, and trials of this kind would increase their boldness to speak for the truth. The victory of innocence would then belong to the truth alone, and not to its ministers. But now every danger from enemies outside is joined by the murmuring of those within the household, and to these is added, thirdly, the sickness of human knowledge, in the hardship of times that have taken on inner troubles, together with the wickedness of disobedience that has gained mastery over many. Already the Apostle's saying has received its due fulfilment, that in the last times people will be lovers of self, and the rest of the passage. The many other things that the Holy Spirit foretold

many generations ago are now being fulfilled in deed by the sons of disobedience, and it has become hard to stand firm. Yet through these very things the success of our faith is shown. For to whom does the praise of acclamation not belong, if not to the one who, amid the blows of despair, steers the ship of faith by the anchors of his preaching and fills his city with the rich profit of the commerce of spiritual life? For against such a peril of barbarian storms, O father holy in all things, the diligence of your zeal has held out for many years, and you have been able to show the powerlessness of all the satanic schemes of the bodily demons. By this name it seems right to me to call the wicked. For even that ruler of the air possessed a superior nature when he was created by the good Creator, but it was his wickedness against God that attached this name to him. Consequently the heirs of his lordship also seize the inheritance of his name for themselves on every side. Against such wicked demons, the enemies of truth, and against the foolish and disobedient partners in their wickedness, with all the impudence of their madness, the fire of your divine zeal burned through the night [?]. To the brightness of its flame it added the wickedness of their audacity as fuel, so that it put no stumbling block in the way of truth for those who are glad to delight in the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ. So, amid the warfare of the enemies, the murmuring of the household and all the necessity of the time, the glory of your zeal triumphs with praise from God. May he in his goodness exalt your honour by his grace, for the comfort of his true servants, for many years. Amen.
3. To a certain physician, concerning news of an illness.

To the lover of God, our honoured brother Mar Sergius, Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. Our common nature, O our brother, [?] is able through the pleasantness of nourishment to turn the very same things to profit, whether by change and increase for the growth and upkeep of the body, or by producing the painful ailments that befall it. In the same way familiar sufferings afflict the bodies and the souls of us all through the hard diet [?] of adverse and painful reports from the Enemy. How, or by what necessity, did it come about that I, with all here who love you, was forced into great distress when we received the report of your illness and of those you love? The weight of our longing pressed on us all the more because no other good report quickly reached us to counter the adverse one. So hasten, O our brother, to let us know now how the grace of God's goodness is guiding you. Great joy will then dwell in our good desire, which longs to hear of your well-being. And when we are filled with comfort over your recovery, we will give thanks with you in everything to the mercies of God toward you. May he in his goodness keep you from all harm always. Amen.
4. To a great and renowned monk, concerning the hard events that took place against the faith.

To the father holy in all things, Mar Ḥnanishoʿ, your son Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. O father, the mystery of iniquity has already begun to press on, and the birth of wickedness is awaited amid the hard pangs that bring it forth. It is now the time, as we suppose, for chastisement to prevail over all. See the darkness of the many troubles the time holds for us, and the famine of the goods that sustain human life. The root of Christianity has begun to dry up in the scorching heat of the lack of priests, who water [?] the shoots of the beloved plant. The destroyer has gained strength in the town [?] together with the unworthy. On top of all this came the departure from bodily life of that head who loved the faith, and at the same hour came the arrival of that Magian persecutor of the fear of God. Many were distressed and even despaired of their lives, not [only] of the danger of suffering [?], and these became an evil spectacle to the many who discern, along with other matters that make the signs of the discerning harder concerning the inner breach [?]. They proclaim plainly enough, as I said, the mystery of iniquity and the revealing of the wicked one. But worse for the discerning than anything that afflicts them is the slumber of negligence that has gained mastery over those who uphold the truth. What, then, can strengthen weak men like me, so that they may be granted a little comfort? Only this, which I have long wanted to do: to send words of sighing in a letter to you, head who loves God. When I stir the compassion of your fatherhood with the memory of the inner breach, I may quickly find the gift

of comfort from the visitation of God's goodness through the petition of your prayer, and from darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see. For the good labour for the salvation of all greatly befits the love of God of your fatherhood; through it you have reached, from the height of your days, the fullness of praise, so that you may be glorified [?]. In conclusion, then, [?] I ask that the remembrance of my weakness not be missing from the prayer of your fatherhood, so that I may be worthy to spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God.
5. To the teacher of Arbela, because he asked after his welfare with marks of honour in a letter to the head of the monastery, and concerning his diligence for imprisoned confessors.

To the one excelling in all things, the teacher of divine things, Mar Daniel, Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. O modest one, with a feeling of comfort I gloriously received the respect shown by your humility, and the benefit of your fine love seemed to me to make me feel, alone and together, the abundant fellowship of those above whom you set me [?]. Since you addressed the community in common, I felt joy at the manner of your [?]. It was not shame at being despised that troubled me as I met it, but the danger of my lack of learning frightened me. I was left in doubt [?], then, by these things, since it seemed fitting to be engaged in both together: in the one I appear as what I am, that is, unlearned; in the other as what I am thought to be, that is, one who flees from vain praise. If, then, it is natural for [streams?] to gather toward the deep,

and for writing [?] to rise by arguments toward the goal we aim at, and for the varied light of the stars toward [?], and for the whole order of change to be governed toward its right cause, so also it is natural for knowledge, which gives birth to many [?] images of thought, to answer with eloquence, as is seen in you more than in all these. How much more, then, if you dare without being ashamed to blend the need of my mind with the commandments of contemplation in the deep and abundant bosom of the knowledge of your wisdom. You were raised to that renowned rank of theologian, and in the nature of your eloquence you were blended with the natures of [?] and established as heir; and always, as now, you have philosophized about spiritual things. The order that was hidden from custom [?] you show to be more lovable, and by taste [?] the sweetness of the laws is fashioned. You fill the need of the pairs [?] of the course of the wise, and command the inner man to do the good of the inner man, which mind, feeling and diligence each perform. And this while he suffers, while he speaks in [?], while he bears the retribution of scourgings, while he toils to do good. [?] the sons of God, while with the chief of the contests he cries out, "if you dare," even to be cut off from Christ, if he could, so that he might make many righteous. To you, then, who are in all things a vessel of eloquence and a cultivator of spiritual seeds, and now also a minister to those in bonds, who love sufferings for the sake of glory; [?] for Christ who is a prisoner, sick, hungry, thirsty, naked; to you who every day, on behalf of all, share in blessed sufferings: with what shall I come before the altar, and repay a fruit worthy of the deed? With blessedness in return for what has been [?], or with praise

hidden in sufferings, or with your humility toward us? No, not even to add strength to your strength by our encouragement, as if a star could add to the sun. For nothing was left for us on your part, I think, that is worthy of prayer, except what belongs to the Lord, that is, the success of his will in you. May he in his goodness bring all the labour of your good works to perfection in the mercies of his grace. Amen.
6. To the believer mentioned above, concerning his trial.

Ishoʿyahb to Sabrōy my brother: peace in our Lord. "For now our salvation is nearer to us than when we believed," says the blessed Apostle. When we are measured by the strength of the trouble that has come upon us toward an increase in the fruits of chastisement, O my beloved, let this very saying of the Apostle be proclaimed, until it pleases the good God to grant a helpful end at the time required. For the earth, mother of all, when it receives in its body the pain of wounds from the drawing of the ploughshare, then yields the most useful fruits. Know then, O my beloved, that we spent most of our days in a luxury that brought losses [?], and like barren land we grew a forest of desires. As for sins, either we were wholly estranged [?], or we sat idle in contempt [?]. Therefore the care of God's mercy cultivates our hardness with ploughing trials and gathers gladdening fruits to help us at the proper time. For they are persuaded on every side, as good disciples, by the Apostle of God, who every day cries to us, saying, "Endure discipline, then, because God is dealing with you as with sons."
May he in his goodness hasten the visitation of his mercies for our salvation. Amen.
7. To his cell-companion at the School of Nisibis.

Ishoʿyahb to Hormizd my brother: peace in our Lord. You have dared a great deal, O modest one, and you have held out a strong support [?] to increase my endurance. Pray, then, in your modesty, that one as receptive as I am may be brought near to all [?] of your wisdom, so that in the course of time [?] of those who love you may be strengthened for you. For when I gladly receive in the body of my thoughts the bites [?] of your youthfulness, I am greatly ashamed, because I was never held back by any change of help [?] from being drawn from the delight that stirs the spirit, while I busied myself breathing [?] toward the commandments in your letter, words that befit your honour. That this can happen if I wish it, you no longer doubt. May God give you wisdom in all things, and strength to keep the joy of love in the might of the Name.
8. To the head of the monastery of Mar Ṣlibā, concerning the troubles after the death of Yazdin.

To the minister of the Lord and worker of righteousness, Mar Sabrishoʿ, Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. As you indeed urge, O pious man of God, I am ashamed that for many days, even at pressing times, I was found [?], so that the love of my [?] mind might be nourished by meeting your face. For it is worthy of diligence

that one who has experienced a man's excellence before being persuaded of it should keep the memory of his piety in unfailing treasuries. For your perfection surpassed my earlier choice by the choice of your will, and so it also seemed to me a fitting debt that, through the weak ability of my own person, I should always repay your love with the wishes it needs. When I consider these things now, too, and at a time that calls for showing a shared and lasting sympathy, I am in pitiable distress [?], as if it were my own person. Meet, then, with strength and enduring power, O modest one, the force of the changes the time holds for you. For it is neither possible nor found that anyone should sail the turbulent deep of this changeable world without being tossed by distressing waves. But you have, more than anyone, a venerable [?] and the banner of salvation, able to hold the ship of your mind steady in the storm of this time. For he who was once plunged [?] into time shook the earth and slew death, and from then on, every day, he throws down the legions of demons when he is faithfully served. How much more will he give you, more than anyone, victory in daily deliverance, as the minister of his holiness. So when you are kept free from all harm, we too will be able to take delight in your affairs without distress, and the thanksgiving due for such care will abound through the many to the glory of Christ. May he in his goodness keep you from all harm. Amen.
9. To a certain friend, after the war of the Romans.
Ishoʿyahb to Sergius: peace in our Lord. Since the storm of war has stirred up in its turbulence the sea

of the world, O my beloved, and in the gusts of the blows of captivity the ships of humanity have been shaken to all the ends of the earth, and only in the clefts of fear has a remnant been left, like the terrified remnant in the days of Noah, the minds of friends are in a tumult of doubt over the hope of what would gladden them. From the confusion of good things, as from the crest of the waves of the deep, we hope for a likeness of health. But the flame [?] of our gladness is not yet secured by sure hope. So take care, O modest one: if you are with us in the life of the body, gladden us with the hope of your health, whether by coming or by letter. Then, when you learn what has passed over us, you will lighten our burden by sharing in comfort. As for us, like a brand plucked from the fire, we give thanks to our Lord, who has spared us in all things, and we pray that we may soon receive your face with joy. May God keep you from all evil. Amen.
[10?] To a certain monk, concerning the death of his superior.

To the father excelling in all things, the honoured Mar ʿAbdishoʿ, Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. The man of God who was able to receive a double portion of the spirit of prophecy, when he sent the prophet of fire to heaven in a chariot of light, mingled Israel's loss with his own grief, and in the plain of [?] he cried out with cries worthy of his grief. Although the promise of his request greatly comforted him [?], his faith triumphed over the trial, and the mantle [?] of the armour of prophecy was led [?] to the ranks of Israel according to the flesh.

For this reason I too lament, for something like this has happened. How are we not compelled on every side, all who fear God, to feel grief for the chariot and horsemen of the spiritual Israel, that is, for the chief of the hosts of the Church's ranks [?], for the strong tower of the spiritual way of life, for those who in a mortal body bear the pattern of the life after the resurrection, for the wall of his divine zeal, which always stood against every attack of evil teachings, for the one holy in all things and pious beyond all, the perfect image of excellence, the blessed father Mar Ḥnanishoʿ? At this time, when all needed him, he has been sent to the place rich in saints. For the pain of that loss is hard, and it creeps into the depths of our natural affections, and in a powerful measure it makes us put on love for those who excel. At times the hope of the promises to come is lifted up, but many times it also struggles against unbelief within faith itself, and so it knows its pain keenly in such pains. Therefore we are compelled, in things like these, to mingle with grief, we who have been left to endure the pangs of bereavement of a spiritual father. For even if he measures out to us not a double portion of the might of his zeal, but only the brightness of his rays, as to a second Elisha, it is enough to cover with the light of his truth the darkness that presses on us, and, without grief, to give rest in the calm of faith to those who trust in the good inheritance of the holy [?]. And since such an anointing is still hidden from the perception of bodily men, God is faithful in his promises, for the Lord will not forsake his people, nor abandon his inheritance. It is therefore necessary that when, from the place of the sons of the prophets, he looks toward the division of the Jordan, which helps toward the fulfilment of the promises, then he will cast from us the fear of doubts

and we will be strengthened in the hope of our truth as by a breastplate of iron. We will show at the time required a boldness worthy of the glory that is in our Lord, and the goodness that hastens to many will, through many, abound in thanksgiving to the glory of Christ. Amen. As for me, O pious man of God, the departure of that holy head from bodily life at this time has dealt a blow from [?], and it was still shaking in the doubt of my thoughts, and flight from everything seemed to me what would benefit my need. In constant departures [?] the feeling is stolen away from afflicting [?]. I beg your piety, then, to pray, and to strive all the more that the bitterness [?] of the trouble that overtook us may be swallowed up in our joy, and that in the success of your good works the glories of all may increase. Remember me too every day, so that through the petition of your prayer I may be found worthy of the mercies of God, and may soon delight in the gladdening meeting with your face. Let the greeting of my goodwill be given, with the kiss of your love, to the blessed fathers and the holy brothers with you. All the holy ones here greet you.
11. To the brothers on Mount Izla, concerning the death of their head.

To the minister of God, the pious father Mar Ḥabibā, with the blessed fathers and holy brothers who hasten with him in the service of the Spirit, the son within the love of your fatherhood, Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. I never expected, O pious men of God, that, humbled [?] by the onslaught of adversities, I would see the eagerness of my will [held back] from running toward the fair love. And in all this it was so humbled that not only

was it deprived of conversation with you, which is so profitable, but it was also robbed of all the comfort of the gladdening hopes a letter brings. The force of the grief pressed on me all the more because on your side too, no less than on mine, the possibility of the matter was cut off. For I hope in our Lord that soon I will find the remedy for all of it in meeting your love, which fills every consolation. As for the distresses of trial that I have endured inwardly until now, let them be left, one by one, for long accounts, in which our meeting face to face will be delighted with joy, if God helps. But since the display of daily adversities covers our weakness without success in anything, think of me, I ask you, and comfort my need with the goodness of your care, and [tell me] how the grace of God's goodness is guiding your life since you sent the man of God to heaven and placed that exalted head, victorious in all things, in the order of the saints. For whom does the glory of blessedness befit more than you, who fill the kingdom of heaven with holy ones of the Most High? You taught the orders of the service of the Spirit, in the manner of angels, to the people of the East, and they rose from the fleshly world to incorruptible life. In you, as in pure gold, they fixed the image of their ways, and the shining image of the fear of God, the profit of their diligence, is in you through the fruits of their labours. For of these and such men, while that blessed head, holy in all things, our blessed father Mar Babai, was [among you], who among those once renewed in the spirit of their mind, as the Apostle commands, would not reckon a [?] departure at the needed time worthy of blessedness, and the rest of the praise for the times to come? For even though he mingles with joy

[?] bodily grief, since those in need always lean on a natural support, yet the display of what has happened turns aside the force of grief. For it lies in God's hands, as it is written, to raise up even from these dead stones, in every generation, living men fit for the consolation of his true servants. I trust, too, that the blessing of his goodness will be kept abundantly in you to the end, as a display of his love toward his holy ones. Remember, then, the days, day after day, in which you endured great contests in sufferings for the sake of truth, and became a spectacle in the struggle against the corrupters of the faith, and endured with joy the persecution of [?], and did not yield to the veil of error, which even by a small word darkens the light of truth; but by revealing the truth you made the boldness of good confession shine before all. Even the mouths of enemies are compelled to proclaim the victory of your testimony. By these daily memorials you have gained, in every place, witnesses of your steadfastness in the holy Church: to keep the uprightness of faith in fitting confession, and to excel in the practice of the spiritual way of life that the holy fathers handed down. These things you will fulfil wholly [?] with God's help, as I trust. There is nothing, then, lacking for a good and perfect hope, nor anything worth praying for in what the capacity of strength requires; rather, everything in every memorial gives me joy. I pray only that such good may abound in the world, for the glory of our truth and the thanksgiving of the righteous. I beg the love of your fatherhood that the memory of my weakness be kept in the prayer of your piety, so that I may be worthy to spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God.
12. To the brothers on Mount Izla, concerning the delay in replying and concerning adverse news.

To the ministers of God and diligent workers of excellence, the pious father Mar Ḥabibā with the blessed fathers and holy brothers who together on Mount Izla, in the inheritance of father Abraham, are glorified in the service of the Spirit, the son within the love of your fatherhood, Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord. I entreat you, O pious men of God: ever since I began to thirst for your love, I have written in pain, because the hardship of the adversities that occurred was able to cut off the eagerness of my will from meeting your faces. Inwardly I was pained and torn [?] by grief, because we could not meet one another for a long time, not even by letters from afar. From then on, from the time I wrote, you have been silent. On my side alone, as it seems, the weight of grief has grown, partly because of [?], partly because of longing, and partly because of my extreme faintness of heart. And while I was thus waiting for hope about your affairs in the time that has passed, O pious men of God, the storm of my sins snatched me away to the deep of Seleucia, and I have been compelled to stay there a long time, until now. This was from nothing else than the law of love, as it were. For the increase of [?] friends every day added to my delay there, especially since my business before him was being drawn out in the hope of some benefit. But when I appeared, I rejoiced eagerly.
13. To a certain monk who was called to the headship of another monastery.

Ishoʿyahb to Paul my brother: peace in our Lord. I heard about your coming, and I also read what you wrote to me. In casting doubt on your coming you did not do well. For this does not befit one who always hopes in his Spirit [?] in all the changes that befall him. But perhaps, because of your great simplicity of habit, you count your moving from place to place as a matter of manners, ways and reputation. Do not think of it like that; rather, take with you to every place a stranger's [?] and a humble mind, and they will go with you in all your affairs, and you will be at rest. Commit your soul to our Lord always, as you indeed do. Let your will always be in the will of God, so that he may guide you in all your affairs in the way of his truth. Lean on the truth and fear nothing. For those who speak the truth can rebuke even the kings of the earth, especially if they also do the truth they speak. Do not be a teacher to the brothers with you as if on your own authority, but only one who reminds them of the commandments of our Lord and the teachings of the fathers. When you have reminded them, urge them to keep them. If they consent, govern them in love. If they quarrel, give them notice of your departure. If they urge you to stay, urge them to keep the commandments. If they do not keep them, let them know at once that you are not obliged to stay with them. If you must leave, set before them openly a fair reason, and leave without anger and without blame, so that you do not leave behind you a just complaint for hasty tongues. All these things are so as not to put up with

disobedience. But if they become obedient to the profitable commandments, there is no greater wealth of excellence for them and for you. Learn more, so that you may give more and gain [?]. More than anything, devote yourself to teaching about love, and give the first example of it in yourself, so that the word may be better received and profit within may increase. As for the old customs of the place, which already need to be changed, contend against them little by little. First persuade them of what is greater, and then abolish what is lesser, so that when the things required are judged by comparison with one another, the excellence of what you say will grow. If they keep it, they will know that you were a teacher of good to them; and if they do not, they will know that they despised the good. And finish by saying: "I return with profit, and with profit I depart." Count as profit whatever your conscience [?] bears witness to. Let your mind not rush ahead in anything, but bring everything into the court of your thoughts, examine it justly in the fear of God, and hold to what is right. And may the God of peace give you peace in your dwelling, and make you perfect in every good work to do his will, so that you may be strengthened with all strength according to the good pleasure of his will, to the glory of God and our encouragement. Pray for me too, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. Our brother Mar Ḥnanishoʿ and the brothers with me greet you. Give greetings to the brothers with you, and urge them to pray for my weakness.
14. To a certain teacher, concerning sickness and poverty.
To the man of labours and diligent works, of upright learning, the chaste and God-loving Mar Ḥaḥya [?], priest and teacher: Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord.

O lover of God, I received and read your letter to me, which showed in great measure a littleness of love. I thanked our Lord for your health. But this is littleness of love: to lay down praise and compliments with many persuasive words and to send our friends a display of our mind. With others, for the sake of new friendships, it is perhaps fitting to write or say such things as a small courtesy. But if we grant such things to someone face to face, we do not entirely escape the fear of flattery. So, O lover of God, the constancy [?] of our mind is proof enough of the truth of our love. And we trust that with God's help it will remain unshaken for ever. Now I have heard, O lover of God, that you have fallen into severe poverty over money. I have also heard that you have fallen ill and that your body has grown very weak, and that both these things have left you distressed in mind. A thought like this does not suit your years, O chaste one. How can it seem to you that a man who has shown his diligence for seventy years is weak now? For a soul that hopes in God, fear over just one of these things is itself a sickness, and how much more for a teacher of the truth! I think it was out of smallness of soul that you were seized by both of these. Your confidence about the health of your body and the goods outside the body rested on poor hopes. That is why the Spirit of the Lord blew upon both, so that the hope for both might be placed in the Lord. So hope in the Lord as befits your mind, and bear calmly the medicine of poverty and sickness: the one as Lazarus did, the other as Job did, and both until the glory that comes from God, who in his providence will crown

the honour of your old age gloriously with the fair longing of your mind, to the glory of God and to our encouragement. As for me, I have set out on the journey that you know about. So pray that it may be ordered according to the will of our Lord. And may I see you in peace, in the joy that comes from God.
15. A defence to the Catholicos on behalf of the leaders [?], concerning the flight.

To the holy one, in all things our pious father, Mar Ishoʿyahb, Catholicos and Patriarch: Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord. I think that in what I have already said, my lord, I have given a clear enough picture of the distress my mind suffered in the events that took place, and of why the outcome did not match the aim but came to be treated as a matter of explanation [?]. For the outcome that certain people set for the suffering before they compelled us [?] is plain to many. But as it seems to me, in this affair the force of the matter was falsified. Not only did it miss the aim, it even turned endurance into its opposite [?]. For through many past days I bore the proof of my endurance, and I held on in hope until compulsion grew sharp. When I was compelled by force, I gave up explaining my conduct by letter so that I might appear in person before your fatherhood. In this monastery, as in the precinct of the church of Kokhe, I am waiting quietly to hear whatever God commands through the mouth of your piety. Openly and with just [?] cause I have presented myself at your feet to show the suffering of my mind. Take care, then, O chaste one: as you do for your servant what befits you for the glory of God, give me life too as a beloved son, and make abundant joy dwell among all who fear God in every place. For it falls to you more than to anyone to pursue, and fitting zeal

for the truth. Many causes are pressing [?], and the consciences of many are inflamed over them. May the Steward of our good things make the truth of his teaching prosper in your hands, to the glory of the community. Amen.
16. A greeting to a friend at Tumalna [?].

To the honoured one, in all things our pious father, Mar Theodore, bishop: your son Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord. If the governing will prospered in every wish that is full of fair things, O our father, nothing would have kept the longing of my mind from being fed by a meeting with your fatherly love before anything else. For I owe this both by rank and by nature. By rank, because of the commendation made earlier by letter, which by the beauty of its composition [?] bound the members of my household to your fatherhood [?]. By nature, because of the bond [?] of their gentleness, since they belong to the spiritual orders that praise the one truth of the community in a single perfection of mind, and are the diligent sons of the same good inheritance of the blessed fathers. So such a fellowship is worthy of praise among the wise, and because of it I am bound to hurry to meet you in person. Contrary obstacles have arisen and have delayed the time of my coming there, but I hope in our Lord to come quickly. And my hope will succeed if, through the request for prayer, I receive the help I need. But I am delayed a few days until I visit the outlying places of Athor, beyond this convent where I am. I confess that I deserve to be harried in this way. For I have never done anything worthy of the goodness

of God toward me, and so I am now reaping the fruit of my negligence in daily turmoil. But thanks be to God, who orders everything for our help. I beg you to pray that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God.
17. To the brothers in the monastery of Izla who were driven away [?] by their brothers and wronged.

To the chaste brothers on the mountain of Izla, who in the inheritance of our father Abraham are diligent in spiritual service, lovers of God and labourers in virtue, my lords and brothers Habib, Dazuzai [?], Gregory, Luke, Arzishoʿ [?], Stephen, Yazdin, Bardoq, Simeon, and the chaste brothers with them: Ishoʿyahb your brother, peace in our Lord. O strong men, as the length of years shows, I placed great hope in you, a false hope as I now feel [?], because I raised my confidence in you above every fear. I never expected that I would see you brought low by the obstacles that arise, as I do now, since many proofs had shown that victory belonged to you [?] in the trials that Satan is accustomed to work through the enemy within. But now I have written to you twice and you have kept silent and answered not a word, so I perceive perhaps the evil I had feared, which I have now heard has befallen you. Because of this I cry out in pain and raise in lamentations [?] a voice of tears. Who has taken that desirable vineyard, which flourished with the fruits of righteousness, broken down the hedge of its watchfulness, and left it to be trampled by all the

unclean feet of the wicked? Who has shaken that strong tower, fortified on every side, as if by secret undermining, and brought the pride of its strength down to the ground? Who has come against the ranks of the spiritual warriors, who many times won the victory of truth in trials from the hands of powerful rulers, and now in the midst of peace at home has produced schism at home, and as with a sharp sword has removed the commanders from the places assigned to them? Who has entered the fold of the strong man, stripped him of his armour, overcome him and seized his goods? To speak more plainly: who has wretchedly forced the beloved sons of Abraham the upright, the good heirs of Dadishoʿ the righteous and the chaste disciple of the glorious Babai, to suffer [?] at one another's hands today? They had everything in common: faith and conduct, soul and word, and every good deed. But it is clear that an enemy has done this, that is, the wicked demon who hates mankind. From the beginning he sowed the seed of disobedience in paradise. Afterwards, in the field, he brought forth the first murderer. In every generation he has inflicted evil wounds on our nature through evil servants. Now too he boasts not a little, for he has fallen upon you as upon a peace beloved by God, split your concord with the sword of his craft [?], and is suddenly carrying off your truth in triumph [?]. So I tremble, O pious men, that at Izla, as at Dothan, I shall stand and see the chaste brothers plotting craftily against the one whom Israel loved. They draw him up out of his cell as out of a pit and send him far away, as into Egypt, under an unjust excommunication. And not him alone, but also the one who, like Reuben, took pity, and the one who, like Judah, devised a way out [?]. Over these things my heart is broken

and my frame [?] has trembled, all the more because the hatred is still growing. This evil is pleasant and makes one numb: the sons of Jacob persist in making their loved ones suffer, and do not foresee the revelation in Egypt before the day of shame, from which there is no escape. Know then, O brothers, that the discerning find the cause [?] of your fall more hateful than all this. Friends grieve and enemies laugh. And it pains me more sharply than anyone, as I wait for the evil that is coming, for I had thought that I had you as pillars of confidence in the struggle against it. Now hands are slack and the thoughts tremble and grow weak. Who will ask health of the sick, strength of the weak, or harmony of the divided? Who would not be filled with despair [?] when he sees the leaders of the battle wretchedly trampling one another? It would be bearable if they took a real person [?] as the cause of the disturbance, for then the evil would at least be open. But they attack [?] one another's good name secretly, as if in the dark. Does the one who was persecuted not have the same faith as you, and indeed in greater measure? Does the one who was persecuted not have the same love, and indeed in greater measure? Does the one who was persecuted not have the same zeal, and indeed in greater measure? Has the one who was persecuted not fought the same contests for the faith, and indeed in greater measure? Does the one who was persecuted not have the same power of word and of teaching, persuading on behalf of the truth against those who once tried to force you to fall away from it, and indeed in greater measure? How then, my lords, can your quarrel be justified [?], when you had no real cause for the schism you have openly made? But perhaps

you will say that he was rejected by the heads of the church, and that this is why you too treat him as a stranger. But you ought to have examined the matter. Until now you have shared sufferings with one another, and as members of one body you ought to have kept the order of harmony. If you had wished, you could have shown the strength of your love to the metropolitan and the patriarch by gentle persuasion. And if it was necessary to deal kindly with your brothers in whatever way the governors of the church thought fitting, you should have been found ready and eager to plead for the one who had been dismissed, all the more since you yourselves are held by the authorities on the very same charge. But now you have not only failed to hurry to Seleucia [?] so that the patriarch might grant you [?] peace; you have not even entreated the metropolitan on his behalf. Instead you have acted like a bitter leaven [?] that spoils bread for no reason. And while he was being released by the governors of the church on another ground, you added fresh accusations of wrongdoing, pouring vinegar on top [?]. Do you not know that you will be called to account [?] in the end, if not now then on the day of reckoning? So awake, O pious men, and consider that we stand by the mouth of the canon. We are like water poured out on the ground that cannot be gathered up again. In all of Satan's schemes there is nothing that is not under your power, if you are willing to overcome. There is no transgression that has no remedy, if you are willing to take care. There is no stumbling that cannot be mastered by persuasion, if you love peace. Be reconciled with one another, then, and examine the cause of the disturbance, and see whether

it comes from the working of error or from human strife. If you think it through well, you can know what is pleasing to God. Do that and live. Turn from wrath and rest from anger, and do not be eager to do evil, for the wicked will perish, but those who hope in the Lord will inherit the earth. Know above all that when the passion [?] of wrath takes control of the understanding, it first strips a man of every virtue, and then it can easily drive him to strike his fellow over trifles. He can no longer tell the fair from the hateful or gain from loss, but only rushes like a madman to do harm. So beware, O brothers, lest you be found captives to such an evil. For I have heard that you have already done something, a shattering blow, that shakes the discerning. They say that in a letter of injustice you confirmed a sentence against your brothers. Alas, alas for harsh injustice! Alas for barbarous tyranny! Alas for lawless excommunication! Who listened to that injustice? Did he ever before listen to anything else that served the glory of God? Did his thoughts rouse him against the heresies that fight against the truth? Did he shake the foundations [?] in the struggles against those who corrupt virtuous ways of life? Did he rebuke, by writing and by word, those who under the various guises of empty error are scheming to enter the church of God? Or is this perhaps his only course, from first to last: to give his brothers, his mother's sons, a demonstration of his zeal through excommunication, the very men whose glorious truth even the mouths of their enemies are forced to proclaim? If, then, all of you, O merciful men, agreed to commit this injustice,

thanks be to the gift of God that he did not give you authority in his church over the perfect ones of the flocks! Otherwise you would easily have struck down those in need of correction, if this is the patience you show in correcting your brothers. But if only one man listened to it, and all of you were persuaded to consent, then we have an evil prospect: that in other matters too he will do you great harm, until every evil is complete, and before all else by the disgraceful [?] affair of Babai bar Yoyan [?], which either you have already suffered or, as I think, you will soon suffer. Until now he has thrown into confusion the ways of the Lord, and your own ways as well. Now, as if spurred by the eagerness of your zeal, he will treat with even greater contempt the saints who sleep in Christ, who left you the record of their virtuous course as to diligent heirs. And see, they will now suffer cruelly at your hands, like fathers under the ban, because you were not able to attain the excellent wisdom that was theirs, which was expected [?] of you. So they are truly blessed, and also wretched. Blessed, because in all the glory of virtue they were made perfect in the contests of righteousness and departed to our Lord. Wretched, because they left their monasteries as an inheritance to such sons. I was compelled to say these things by the painful grief that came upon me when I heard what you had done. Yet I do not think it possible that this evil has overcome the whole assembly of your brotherhood like a weakness, and that not even a few among you are found who love peace together with truth, and who counsel what is good. But if, God forbid, this evil has gained power over all of you,

like sleep over those sunk in it, then hear me, I beg you, if only as a voice that wakes you from your sleep. Awake, then, awake, O brothers! Awake with zeal as in the former days, and put on the strength of the arm of the Lord. Do not throw away the boldness you have, for a great reward is stored up for it. Remember the former days, in which you endured a great struggle in sufferings for the truth, in reproaches and afflictions, and became a public spectacle; and you also became partners with those who endured these things, and accepted with joy the plundering of your possessions, knowing that you have in heaven a reward that is excellent and does not pass away. This, then, all this glory of virtue, is what Satan is scheming to take from you through the enemy within. He laboured greatly over long years, yet he could not harm you through foreign hands as he wished. He has stirred up many against you at all times, men who were strong in power and prosperous in the world, and they perished as they perished, while you have remained as you are, in surpassing glory, until now. Nor could that hater of mankind raise up from your own sons a servant fit for his will, until he went far away from you and found a leprous demon called Isaac. He mixed him with the fumes [?] of his wickedness and blended him into your peaceful community, to his own destruction and to your harm. In him he has found a diligent servant who has fully accomplished his desire, and Satan, the enemy of our race, expects to sift [?] you. So, O pious men, may the Lord not grant his desire to unjust deeds by your hands, and may his scheme not succeed. Rather, let the injustice of his lips cover him, so that he may burn in the coals

of his sin. As for you, shake yourselves free of the dust of hatred, wash yourselves clean of the grime [?] of enmity, and awake from the sleep of negligence. Walk as children of light. Be steadfast in the truth of God, as God is steadfast toward you [?]. Guard the deposit of your fathers carefully, so that you may be the heirs of their holiness and not be put to shame before them on the day of testing. Go out after your brothers and gather them in. And if you must suffer for them, do not hold back [?] until you have made them your companions in the monastery and partners in love. For an evil time is coming upon us before long, in which you will need many helpers, if you truly love the faith and love the truth. Otherwise you will have lost every virtue at a stroke. Remember, then, O sons, my weakness [?], me, the partner of your love, and judge [?] well of me, as I also do of you. Answer me in writing with the true thoughts of your minds on everything I have written to you. Write to me as you think best, all of you together or each one separately. For I am to you now what I was before, that is, a son and a brother, and in every way a sharer [?] in your deeds and words, in all that pleases the will of God and rescues from injustice everyone who calls on the name of the Lord. May he in his goodness make you perfect in every good work, so that you may do his will. Be steadfast in our Lord.
18. To the brothers in his monastery, concerning the appointment of the abbot.
To the lovers of God, my beloved and dear brothers, Simeon

and John and Qamishoʿ and Bar Denḥa and Daniel and Bar Zasorin [?] and Bar Nun and Ishoʿzkha and Aphnimaran and all the holy brothers in the monastery of Beth ʿAbe, each by name and all alike: Ishoʿyahb your brother, peace in our Lord. I was expecting, O brothers, that out of the zeal of your love I would be informed of the glorious departure of that holy abbot from this life in the flesh to the harbour of eternal life. If I had not been fully persuaded of the custom of the community, and deeply bound by love for the place of my upbringing, I might easily have taken offence at such neglect, not for the sake of rank or title, but for the sake of brotherhood and of being raised in the same customs. For the ways in which you fell short in this matter of the law of divine love, O God-loving brothers, may our Lord be forgiving and merciful, and may he always confirm your hearts in the love of truth. Amen. Now I have heard that you are still caught up in disputes [?] over the matter of the headship, and that you have not faithfully and with one accord carried out what the holy father handed to you by word of mouth as an everlasting testament, but that other wishes are already appearing among you. I wanted to come to you myself so that counsel might be taken together in a way that would help the community and glorify the holy name of God. Since this was not possible, because I have already set out on my journey to the patriarch, I thought it best to address you in a hasty letter according to the law of spiritual love. Remember, then, O pious men, me, the partner of your love and fellow nursling of your customs. Necessity, I think, demands that these things be recalled, since the affairs of brotherhood are clearly sick. Why

has the title of bishop made me a stranger to you? Why has the laying on of hands for the priesthood separated me from the fellowship of the community? Why has a change of place produced a change of mind? In the things that help the community and increase the glory of God, which of you has ever intended, spoken or done more than I? I speak as a fool: whatever any of you dares in matters that concern the order and honour of your house, I dare too, and not in equal measure but in a more praiseworthy way. Why then, in this present matter, which deserves care more than any other, have you neglected custom [?] and failed to call me, your brother, to the counsel of the community when it was needed? For it was fitting that the living testament should be honoured, which our holy father made with his blessed mouth, in a clear word, a few days before his departure, concerning who was fit to take his place in his ministry. As I heard, he gave that charge on the day of his departure as well. He was afraid that something might suddenly befall him and take him away, so that he would be prevented from saying what he meant to do, so beforehand he entrusted the word about this to me privately. For he did not think you would be persuaded to do anything after his departure without me, in the way you have now strayed from what is required. I was keeping our blessed father's word in my mind until its proper time, but the goodness of God, which guided him peacefully along the way of life, gave him peace of mind to tell it to you as well on the day of his departure. So it is as though you remain at his side in lasting peace, and he is already your head and governor. Since you have the one whom he set apart and appointed as your head, you have rightly obtained a head

and governor. Let no one think, then, that he left him and departed without the hidden armour of prayer. From the moment he set his heart on him and appointed him by word, he committed the disciple of his piety into the hands of God. If anyone of his own will estranges himself from this man's care, let him fear that he may lose the help of the righteous man's prayer. And if he even plans something against him, which of the discerning will not regard him as contemptible and despicable, quite apart from the choking anguish of soul that gnaws [?] at him without success? God forbid that anything of the kind should ever happen or be heard of among the pure sons of the righteous father, the chaste disciple of the holy abbot, my beloved brothers and the sons of my upbringing! Let there be among them only what is good and close to life, what brings help to the community and glory to the name of the Lord. Take care, then, my beloved brothers, of our God-loving brother Mar John the priest, whose virtue has been tested over seventy years less a few: thirty of them in unbroken [?] solitude, and the rest before that in the well-ordered life of the school. And to you, and above all to the elders and honoured among you, he was a receptive and teachable companion of our blessed father. Now, on top of all this, he has been crowned with the crown of headship by our father's command. Since he has been chosen by God with an excellent election, receive him in the Lord with all joy, as pure sons of God. With your hands and your lips, and still more in your hearts, confirm the headship to him with the help of God. And may the God of peace be with you and keep you without disturbance in the dwelling of your sojourn all the days of your life. And may Christ dwell in your inner man

through faith, and in your hearts through love, with your root and foundation made firm, so that you may be able to attain, with all the saints, the hope of eternal life, by the goodness and mercies of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever. Amen. But since the enemy of our good things is accustomed to sow the seeds of his cunning in pure fields, there is reason to fear that among you too, as in the company of the apostles, a stumbling block of rivalry may be thrown down. So take care, my brothers: if any of you is overtaken by such folly and breaks your harmony by refusing to obey the God-loving abbot whom our Lord has set over you, then you who are spiritual, restore him in a spirit of humility, until he is set free from the snare of Satan in which he has been caught to do his will. And may you be made perfect in one spirit for the work of righteousness, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling, to the glory of God and to our encouragement. I know well the many obstacles that usually arise in matters like these. And since I am not staying here, I cannot look into each obstacle that arises among you and supply, as far as I am able, the help needed to correct it. So I am compelled to write you a word of decision, not as a head and ruler, but as an elder brother. If anyone contends against the God-loving abbot, who by the command of our master was appointed over you by the will of God, let him not remain in the community of Beth ʿAbe, so that he does not disturb his brothers and harm himself. Let him move, in calm and in peace and without anger, to a place where he can find rest and profit. And if he happens, in his foolishness, to answer this word with something about me, saying, 'Who

is this man who has commanded us to do these things?', let him learn afterwards from the events themselves and be persuaded, if he fears God. He will indeed need a little repentance to recover the confidence of the children of peace. Let such a man pursue peace and the building up of one another. Let these few words I have written be enough for you to know how my mind longs for your good, and that this is my whole care: that you may live well and speak well, so that God may be glorified in you and I may rejoice as well. I have made known by letter what was fitting about this matter to our God-loving father, Mar Metropolitan. And with God's help I will also tell our father Mar Patriarch about it in person. So you too, knowing these things, be eager together to keep the harmony of the Spirit in the bond of peace, and abound in the work of the Lord. May he in his goodness make you perfect in every good work, so that you may do his will at all times. Amen. And pray for me too, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God.
19. A short admonition to the one newly [?] installed as head of the monastery.

To the chaste and God-loving, our honored brother Mar Qamishoʿ: Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord. I received and read the letter you sent, and I also rejoiced at the arrival of the brothers here with me. I gave thanks to our Lord for your well-being. As for my coming to you, as you asked: the many affairs here hold it back, together with the obstacles that lie between us. But if a door is opened to me

in the Lord, I am ready to come. Now, about the things that are being worn down, as it were, by the will of the community in the hope of [?], as you wrote to me: do not be quickly shaken, like people who are untried or of little hope. For he is faithful in his words and rich toward all who call on him. Only let it be in peace, as it is written. If it goes as requested, through [?] changes, it is a grace to accept it; and if otherwise, and together with the community, that too is a grace. As for what you also wrote to me about the weakness of [?] in the service of the brotherhood that has been laid upon you: do not be afraid at all of what happens. Our ways do not prosper through ourselves, however diligent we may be, but through him who is able beyond all things to act for us, and beyond what we ask and think. So do not be shaken by any word or any voice. If you have set yourself to the work of many, then endure, be patient and long-suffering, even to the point of what befell Ezekiel, if it comes to that. For the world is not stripped of such things, so long as we are all human beings and children of the earth. It is possible to warn and to admonish, but not at all to strike or be struck, while the rule of the Spirit guides you and those under you. If anyone stumbles, the Lord heals him. For the children of peace are known, and so are those who want to strike; and the Lord knows those who are his. So hope in him and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the earth. And as for the hope that rests on any human being, turn back to the Lord and live. As for the account of the conduct of our blessed father, the excellent one, which you urged me to write: I am kept from it for the present. For there is no respite [?] from the many daily [?], and this work of writing needs quiet thoughts. As for the neighbor about whom you wrote to me:

if you do not deal him a blow now and take care of the matter, then once his root is firmly set he will trouble you every day. The only one who can set this right, if he wishes, is the metropolitan. And if he neglects it, as is his habit, know that he wanted to see you afflicted. So one of two things must be done: either endure the trial, or [?] to the patriarch. Whichever of these you choose, choose quickly. As for everything else: take care, and again take care, and above all take care, and always take care. Be well, and pray for me.
20. A reply to two persons who wrote to him as one, under a single name.

To the one who nobly prevails through what is noble, the God-loving Mar Yazdshabur: Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord. To you, then, O lover of God, I will write before I write to the one who wrote what I have read, praising the zeal of your reproaches, since you suffer so warmly according to the law of love. As if before the pangs you were again [?] to give birth; and see, from afar both things are plain. But why not only out of order, but also in an orderly way, at risk and [?]? For it is permitted to desire what is good, as it is written; but it is not permitted to carry it out, as this too is written. And so as not to weary you with too many words on such matters, let us state simply the matter in hand. Why, wise man that you are, did you want the stone on which a spiritual building is set to be hurled, as with a sling, by a scabby horn [?] against the coping of the breaches, and to look for the pain of the break, which the sense of hearing, like the blind from afar,

[?]; or perhaps not so, but like iron that [?] is struck by the smoothness of a [?] wind and takes for its maker the form that suits it? I think wisdom would praise this, were it not that the general failure in all things lies under reproach. That you have nothing to blame yourself for in these matters as regards a conscience of envy, I think you are believed. But that it does not happen to some, or rather to all of us, that an obstacle hinders the beauty of the first intention, take my word for it. So help, then, in all good thoughts that bring to completion the thing you love. For you are able to do so in deed, if you are more concerned than all of us to persuade by deed at the proper time. But for you these things are enough, as in suffering. And you, who so forcefully twist the reproach of love as in a dialectical syllogism: how far will you go with reproaches in silence? Or how is it not like a private grievance arising from a just cause? For that praiseworthy force compelled you to take up the shared contest at close quarters: the tongue in place of persons, the soul in place of others, the word in place of the community, and in place of you the repayment of the supposed debt. If indeed, in all these things, the completion of the contest at hand is a grace of the gift to [?], well and good. But if what is now is as it is now, you would be thought not only blameless but rather a loud-voiced reproach. So then, while in your letter you give vent to the spirit of your many reproaches against what is right, do not reproach, as it were, my poverty, or rather the small-mindedness of the fathers of the community, or perhaps the weak [?] of what was well distinguished, well heard, well spoken, and examined well upon well. For this reason, in it

while in it, in the very edge of [?], you feel freely, with a free tongue. What then? Does the service of God's church seem a small thing to you? Then its help would be small as well. God forbid! Turn to the spiritual scriptures and you will find its glory. What then again? He who lies in wait on the road and bites at the heel to throw down the honored: how is the blow that you struck against our God-loving brother John? How is he not only not loved and praised, but is thought to be reproached and disgraced before his acquaintances? Or is it out of harshness? For at one stroke you cast him into the snares of Satan, you showed us to be ministers of sin, and because of the obstacle that arose you proclaimed the servant of God's service to be evil. Enough of this at last, as it is said, that the hungry one [?] be in her hunger. What then again? "I want," he says, "to know the cause of the person's removal." Do you then want to find the birth of something that does not exist? Or perhaps you call an addition to the provision a removal. As for me, not only so; even if another had been brought into the ready ministry in place of this one, I would not have counted it a removal of him. Just as I see Joseph called Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus, among the apostles, even though not in the number of the twelve. And if not so, how much more when not even so. What again? "The agreement of persons who are blameless, in the name of Christianity, would have sufficed," he says. I too say it would have sufficed, if what ought to have been believed had been believed: and even if not with others, but with two or three near at hand among those who make up the full number, even if they were fewer in name. So that the community is not measured by the air,

but by the few who are near rather than by the many others who are far away. Otherwise, who would give counsel about the full number and not be found foolish? What again? "I would like to know, even in secret, the sins that were found." I tell you openly that we have no difficulty in such a finding. But the Lord of our nature does not remove the sinful race from the service of his church. What again? "If someone, or some of those who believe in the full number, hindered its completion, then they ought to have turned back from the one who, as it were, is supposed." Half of the explanation is good, but not the whole of it. For here, sparing you, I heal the wound of suspicion. And take my word for it: there was no Satan, nor any evil occurrence, nor a king estranged from the fear of God. What again? "I see," he says, "that hidden things show forth the outcomes of the affairs, in those things that you said earlier were going to happen. The whole wealth of [?] was dissolved at once, and the debt that hatred extinguishes [?] remains with the one who persuades without the issue of agreements." But I, as a human being, planted in hope, and as a human being I water in hope. And he who causes such a planting to grow gives fruit to the hope of the one who serves God. If it follows him to completion and according to purpose, it is a grace to receive it; and if against purpose and otherwise, that too is a grace of his providence. What again? "It is fitting," he says, "to complete the foundation you laid, so that there may be no room for loose [?] tongues to pour out the accusations of custom." And how then, if we do this, do you suppose that free people will be saved from such accusations? For just as for this, so

for that too the slanderer's [?] tongue is ready. And both, as it were, for good. Or whom among the godly have you seen escape from such tongues? Not the patriarchs, not the apostles, not the prophets, not our Lord, not his Father: clearly, not one. How much less, then, is there consolation [?] for sinners from such things! But these things are enough for you, O bitter [?] slanderer, in answer to those things with which, as with the rod of love, you were striking the one you love in your letter. What happened, how it happened, and why it happened: if you have heard what was said openly, be assured that the hidden things are like it too. Or if you still want to know, my mouth will speak with your mouth, God willing. For now let us only care about this: that as far as is possible we diligently win over the matter from there, our God-loving brother Mar John; so that even if the agreement is not universal, but partial, it may at least be a portion of them. So that no foreign thought may arise in the conscience of those who are set over this, believe me and trust, as I also wrote once. And you too, above all, be zealous, with everyone else, that we may want God's will to be pleasing. And may he, the merciful God, who always does for us more than we ask and think, bring the labor of our zeal to completion, as befits the glory of his name. Be steadfast in our Lord.
21. To him as to him, in him as in him, from him as from him: much peace.

That we judge rightly, even if we are rightly judged, and yet do not humble ourselves somewhat before the Spirit, is not very good; rather, it is not good at all. That justice, as it were, should be upright, when by force

we diminish something. But when one is sufficient for the whole of the contest set before him, then victories are at once complete, even if not with the crown itself. Spiritual, then, is the contest, O you; and spiritual too is its fruit. And many times it is possible, when he rebukes zeal. And who [?]? But those who in the Spirit were entrusted with the vision of hidden things. And who knows whether, as with Samuel, he may rebuke us too [?] in these things? And this, if indeed the present obstacle should succeed, when it can no longer succeed, as I still think. For how could it be that, against conscience, among those who fear God, there should be an obstacle to the fear of God, for anyone who has God? Unless perhaps he is already being purified by shame, of which it is also said that it creates sins; and from it, as from the knot of faint-heartedness, he is swept into a shameful servitude. This, since from it it seemed that he was condemned, to what you condemned, you wrote him something similar, against my [?] calling. And not only similar, but it also befits him to show a spirit of incompleteness, if he wishes to make use of it. But if he turns aside from the way of the fear of God to the straying of license, he does well to despise what you wrote; and he alone does what it is not proper to do. It is good for us, too, to see from afar and by hearing only the things that are done wickedly. Hope, then, in the Lord, O pious men. And if an obstacle should arise from some people that is acted upon, push away from yourselves the stumbling that comes from every side in such things, remembering that we are dust, which now is proud and after a little is scattered. And pray that we may be found worthy of mercy at every hour, and that the goodness of God may guide you in all things. Ended.
22. To the honored, elect and God-loving Mar Yazdgard: Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord.

Just at the close [?] of excellent affairs, the arrival of your letter reached me, O lover of God. And when I was carried far away by the beauty of the style as I read, I withdrew, as was fitting, until by the help of God I was settled in the divine sanctuary in the midst of the field of tares. And after weeping over many [?], I turned to my dwelling place. And rejoicing in the face of the agitation over pressing things, I read your letter again. I praised the theory in it about the soul and its movements and the body and its habits, to the full measure of demonstration. But I was pained, as was proper, by its being carried away toward the one praised, because in a knot, as it were, it was being drawn from the truth toward a foreign likeness. Why, O lover of wisdom, did you carelessly bestow on me, as on someone else, the gift of empty praise? For if you thought that this was the rest of wisdom, then only the beauty of the gift is fine in intent, out of love for wisdom: so that the excellent good may truly be believed in truth, the good by which the weak human side was shown in the beauty of the soul. Apart from this, however, I received with joy the obeisance of your humility, O lover of wisdom; and I confess that you rightly took the lead in the excellent cause. Yours, then, is the primacy, in that it fixed the completeness of excellence by the measure of the spiritual law. For besides being first in the cause, it is fitting also to continue in all things. Yet I regretted the appeal to my knowledge, in those things in which, briefly [?], a restful manner

troubled me, even though the occasions of open praise are pleasant to my weak soul. But as for you, O lover of wisdom, the love of the good persuaded you to let a little falsehood steal into your hearing, and to pour out much of the abundance of love in such gifts toward a weak man who is greatly despised by his own conscience. But I am well astray in those matters in which others think otherwise of me. I confess to God about myself that I am wretched and enslaved to passions. But as for your God-loving soul, which is thus drawn toward the good: may our Lord in his mercies give it true hope. For if this comes about, there will be nothing to shame me; the good will not be lacking, opinion will not be maddened, love will not be changed, choice will not be proved false, joy will not be taken away. Rather, all in all, may there be glory to God, who has been so well displayed by you in respect of the soul. He who by the power of wonder enclosed and gathered this body, such as it is; who made it perceptible to the hidden beauty of rationality; who gave the good of many kinds to be made wise in a single good; who changed this perceptible vessel into hiddenness by a uniting power; who gave us in all and all in us, and in us gave us to know and to marvel at the unity of the power of his creation; who never left himself without witness in us, so that his goodness in us might not be stolen by the deceit of a false likeness; who by vision formerly, by voice afterward, and by word in due time, in the depth of the stillness of knowledge, and at last altogether in a true and complete body, was pleased to keep the good within us without confusion; who gathered the many distinctions of virtue under one high and splendid head and named it love; who through this has now

raised you above my lowliness and handed you the primacy of approach by letter; who gave me to keep the second place in the matter of inquiring after your peace. May he whose hidden power of mercy is at work complete the beginning of our fellowship in the growth of his spiritual law, for the glory of his holy name. May he by his grace complete our weakness in every good work, to do his will all the days of our life. Amen. Give the greeting of my lowliness to whomever you wish, especially to those who are pleasing to our Lord, and specifically to those whose greetings you named to me in your letter. And may the peace of God, which is greater than all knowledge, keep your hearts blameless until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. Ended.
23. To the faithful one of the truth and fearer of God, Mar Ishoʿsabran: Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord.

I received with joy the letter of your love, O lover of God, and I gave thanks to our Lord for your health. And by your abundant wealth of faith you made me rejoice greatly too; for this wealth prevails over [?] in every generation. But that your wise opinion should lean in this way upon a weak and sinful man such as I am did not greatly press me to rejoice; indeed, not at all. For to whom, considering with uncovered face the consciousness of his sins, is praise enough that is spoken of him not as wickedly as his wickedness deserves, if even this is not without danger to accept? And there would be no danger, were it not that he is known to God in one way and thought of by men in another. Yet I was persuaded to reduce somewhat the measure of the explanation,

in that you gave to the scribe Radya, who served you with his skill, the letter to my lowliness, saying that there is an excellent intention which has been formed about me, as about someone in danger, excellent in open hope. May our Lord in his mercies grant that your faith may be made firm on the foundation [?] of truth, and that a hopeful outcome may be given to the eager desires expressed in your letter. For if the goodness of God visits these things, I too may be found worthy, in goodness, of redemption from the wretchedness of guilt. And may it be granted to us in goodness, from the great wealth of God's mercy, that together we may find joy in the fulfillment of excellent things at the due time. May he by his grace strengthen our weakness to do his will all the days of our life. Ended.
24. To the one holy in all things, our pious father Mar Ishoʿyahb, catholicos and patriarch: your son Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord.

May the fear of God that is in you, O our pious father, take note that the good seed, which for a long time was being choked by forest and thorns, has now, through the activity of your fatherhood at this time, been cleansed and has grown, and has begun to rejoice in the light of heavenly things, and has prepared for the angels of God that joy which is in the Gospel. For Shabur, who until now was bowed down by the snares of error into the depths of faint-heartedness, and could not look up rightly to the height of heavenly things through the boldness of confession, has now been loosed from such bonds by the help of God, through the right hand of your fatherhood, and has been made free from the slavery of destruction. And now, standing upright, he goes up

into this great house to which until now he had been restricted. With a soul that was, as it were, new, and a body ready to suffer, he confessed the good confession before many witnesses, and moved the assembly of those who fear God to the glory of the Most High. At once the holy church of Christ here, which is served by the sinful man that I am, spread out her hands and received him, and through participation in the life-giving mysteries gave him the hidden power that sanctifies all, by which the sickness of despair and the pain of [?] grief may be driven out of a man of hope, and he may become a herald of the glory of God and of a splendid confession. And immediately after these things he hastened to go to the [?] that is now near, so that there he may be ready to receive whatever the merciful God in his grace wishes to provide through him. Let your fatherhood therefore rejoice in these things that have happened, and pray earnestly that the completion of all of them may be accomplished for the glory of God. And may he, the merciful God, who extends through his hands every goodness so that it may abound among those who fear him, complete the labor of your fatherhood in every good work, for the glory of his holy name forever. Amen. Ended.
25. To the one holy in all things, our pious father, Mar Catholicos and Patriarch: your son Ishoʿyahb, peace in our Lord.

The cup of our affliction has reached its dregs, as it appears, O our God-loving father, and every way of escape for us has been blocked at the exits of distress. Even refuge has perished for him, as it is written, and there is no one to avenge the tormented.

For the many worms that a wicked deed bred over a long time in the body of the community, and that grew wickedly strong, have at once overcome the many [?], as can be seen, and are now creeping all together toward the head of the community, in which our own mind also is; that is, toward the church of God that is being set in order by God's command, so that it may fill up what remains of its great number in the corruption of its custom, and once it has brought everything to an end it too may come to an end, and the world may rest from its misery. So if you are still in these circumstances, O father, as we hope, and if you are in danger, as we pray you are not, and if by the goodness of God your fatherhood has been granted what remains of comfort in spirit and body: if there is anyone coming this way, order him to write to me, so that, freed from the weight of grief, I may find relief, even if only in the breath of the lower world. For things here are being set in order a little, with the help of God, as the times allow. Yet I am still contending with the times, and over and above its miseries the activity of God's goodness guides my weakness. And it will be a wonder if I am saved here from the end that my sins deserve; for about what lies beyond I have no doubt. Let your fatherhood pray, then, I beseech you, that I may be found worthy of mercy and may find the grace of repentance sufficient to heal my wounds, before I reach the incurable state that befalls many. And may the God of peace cause a dwelling of peace to abide with your fatherhood at all times, with all who are pleasing to his will, all the days of your life.
26. Ishoʿyahb, minister of the church of God that is in [?].
To the beloved of God, the brethren, the monks on the mountain of Alpap, who with a humble spirit [?] in excellent ways of life,

and who make their offering to God who is over all in our Lord Jesus Christ: may your peace abound.

My brothers, beloved of God, I trust that in you too, as in the rest of those who fear God, the power of our Lord's commandment is fully at work. So I have wanted to write to you with a confident mind. I take pride in the fact that the report of your conduct reached me not from strangers' mouths but from our own household, so that my confidence in you may be well founded for times to come. For in my judgment it is quite impossible for a person of excellence, one who truly worships Christ, not to be full of the love of Christ, since this is the mark of discipleship for Christians. Nor can anyone fail to be humble and wise who establishes within himself this spiritual law, the great love which our Lord taught. Nor is it possible for someone not to be calm and gentle who has laid the foundation of his conduct in humility, which is as great as this great commandment. How then could a person come to excellence by any other way, if he has taken up the opposite of excellence, the works of the flesh?
