For wrath, stubbornness and enmity, blasphemy and deceit [?] in an evil mind, wickedly coveting another's inheritance, crossing the boundary set by the fathers with tongue and hand, presuming on one's seniority in years to heap insults on the brethren, and the rest of such things: I do not think these belong to the beloved of God as a praiseworthy portion. They do not even belong to those who, though they have a pagan soul, possess a natural conscience. Let anyone, then, stop thinking himself a disciple of Christ if he does not make it known to all by the fruits of the Spirit that he is one. But if someone

estranges himself from what is excellent, and is not only deprived of it but also wickedly passes judgment on the conduct of the unjust, then, I think, he is wholly dissolved [?] from his own conscience, unless he has been corrupted by the disease of ambition for precedence. The discerning also regard him as an ignorant and unlearned man, because he thinks he acquires not glory from works but works from glory. It is good, then, my brothers beloved of God, to leave the praise of our works to the mouths of others, since by our Lord's command they cannot be entirely hidden. For ourselves, let this be our only occupation: that we believe truly, act truly and teach truly, without showing in any way that we are among those who boast of themselves, but showing ourselves before God, in the openness of truth, to the consciences of all people. In this way we will be no stumbling block to Jews or Gentiles or to the church of God. Let us see to it that we walk carefully, not as fools but as wise, as our master [?] calls them.

So, my brothers, I am sharing these apostolic exhortations with you in common, because the rule of excellence obliges me to. That rule was laid down by no one else but the holy apostle, so that in everything the occasion of stumbling might be removed from the midst, as far as it lies with me. And how is it removed, except by bearing the boldness of fools with abundant gentleness and long-suffering? Such boldness one of your number has now chosen to display with a foolish mind. This man was driven from the toil of the monastic life as if by an enemy, and was forced to hide in the gaping mouth of desolation. Fleeing from submission among his brothers and obedience to his superiors, he concealed himself in the cliff of solitude. And having turned away [?] from a life under no superiors, he chose a path of stumbling

as his dwelling, perhaps so that he might in every way be found a fattened victim, well prepared for the one who delights in people's ruin. This man wanted to stir up this conflict out of season and to no profit, and in harmful agitation hastened into the business of stumbling: rebuke him, my brothers beloved of God. Three times I sent him brotherly persuasion through faithful intermediaries, advising him to value the good of his soul above everything and to leave his grasping way of life. For our Lord [bids us] give up even what is our own, and certainly not to seize [what belongs to others]. When I had urged him at length and achieved nothing, I thought I should let you know too, since you are wise and well able to correct him. If this was done without your knowledge, then now that you know you will be eager to set it right. But if it was done with your knowledge, I know too that he is not the only one among you who loves contention and much [strife]. Even so, it would be more than could be believed that in all that community of many persons there should be found none who love peace and good counsel.

Read, then, in the book of your records, and see who is shown to be the first inhabitant of that place, which is no place of yours. If you remember well, you can see it, since that settlement is not yet old: it belonged to our own monastery and was completed by our own people, and its completion is known to all of you. How then did you see fit to cross our boundaries? I do not suppose that the things of the holy church are now in any way diminished in your eyes. Why then does that foolish man stir up the strife of contention while you keep quiet? Do you not know that great troubles

are born of small causes? Or are you not convinced that a few simple men have thrown many wise ones into confusion? Know this too: if I had not tied the hands of the [?] among us with the bonds of restraint, they would have set upon him with human zeal for acting so boldly against what is right. Help, then, the cause of peace, you chaste men. Rebuke the instigator of war and drive him from our boundaries, and send him back in peace to your fathers' inheritance, as lovers of peace. Give no one any occasion of stumbling. For I, for my part, have heard of the law of spiritual love among you, and I am the first to be zealous for what makes for tranquillity; and you will put an end, by your command, to this trouble you have stirred up. Blessed be the mercy of God, that you have become zealous partners in the labors of his zealous ones. Whenever this helpful persuasion comes from your side, my labor in these matters will not be without fruit; in any case the aim of my zeal is fulfilled in one way or another, as you know. As for the one who troubles you, he will bear the judgment, whoever he is.

However, concerning what I have written to you, send me a letter telling me truly what you think about it. For I want to learn your intention, that it is in the fear of God, not from someone else's words but from your own account. That is why I wrote to you: not because I am too weak to do what is easy enough to be done even by the least of my people, but out of concern for what is fitting, to test the genuineness of your love and to learn by trial whether you fear God in everything. May he in his goodness make you perfect in every good work, to do his will. Be steadfast in our Lord. Peace.
27. To the beloved of God, our honored brother Mar Moses the priest: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

I have received and read what you wrote, my brother, and I thanked our Lord for your zeal in such matters. But I was much pained by the manner of the persuasion and by the cause itself as well. In my thoughts I pursued it to the [riddle?] of it, and I marveled greatly at the contrary [?]: how what then reached only as far as a riddle has now come near to the deed itself. Necessity itself would be astonished in every way if it should happen that the mystery needs [?] the shadow of sin. If even now this is only so in word, why then was it not done cautiously and with me? And if it was undertaken because of some cause, why was it not that cause which came to all of us, which is the cause and the glory of those who possess it, and in which we were also commanded to outdo one another? And if it is neither that nor this, but what was written is true and real as it stands, then woe for the misery of the ruin, that she who was nourished by thousands in every [generation?] should turn toward the mother of hunger to ask for the provision of necessity in a time of need! But it has not been believed, and it will not be believed, that help and strength should flow backwards, from those who are hungry every day to those who are full at every hour. If [the city] still stands in its fair state, and its fair custom even now is to be supplied in every want from the abundance of [its own] needy, then you, my brother, out of excess of hope, or excess of capacity, or excess of care, are sending me the needy as though to someone of that sort. Know first, chaste one, that a lie has crept in under a good [report]. If you had heard the whole of it, you would have written something like these things. That it was a lie you will believe if you learn it, from the place and the custom

first; then from the lack of the necessities of life that is felt by all; and again from the hardship of the distresses [?]. These alone the evil time, in the misery of its state, has cast upon us in the folds of the church. Things I would have been ready to shake off from my hands for them, if I had a living soul, even the wealth of Solomon, had it been given to me. But now, instead of everything, only a sigh can be found from us: a pained heart that draws near to us. As for this gift, I do not think the needy who are settled there are in want of it. For that city, rich in good things, cannot be lacking on this account; it is fitting that she should surpass all in everything. As from the head of the spring that waters her, let her too pour out a draught of help in all good forms, both to us and to all. Even her poverty is enough to make many rich, as it is written.

Still, you did well, my brother, to labor for the souls of the afflicted. You do well if you believe that we are poor in wealth and scant in gifts as well; you do better still if you are not offended to hear that we have sent away empty-handed those you sent to us. Let something reach you from us, if possible: only an eagerness stirred toward what is good. From this, the heart [?] can no longer be in want. And if one takes care in the things we have mentioned, it may be fulfilled in deed too, with the help of God. May he in his grace strengthen our weakness to do his will always, all the days of our life. Amen. Peace.
28. To the faithful one of truth and of the fear of God, Mar Lulina: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.
I received, with [some] interpretation, the letter of your love, O beloved of God,

which was addressed to me by name, but in intent was meant for some other man, someone I am not. Shame at presumption kept me from speaking on account of the name, and shame at causing offence kept me from keeping silent on account of the intent. But after many interpretations I turned to the conscience of my lowliness, gave thanks to the mercy of God, and with a weak soul received with joy the love of your trust: not as I know myself, but as you have been found worthy to believe. For to me, who have no hope and [am full of] my errors, belong misery in everything and a stricken conscience; but to you, a faithful soul, belongs the soundness of loving what is good. So it is that even toward a weak man, who is greatly despised by his own conscience, your faith is fairly placed in the hope of excellence.

It would not be fitting for the sound faith you possess to be emptied, and a broken support such as I am cannot give help; but by the hands of God it is possible even to raise up the dead, for he is rich in his mercies. Fear, then, compels us both to turn to him in prayer, with a single intent born of need. For me, [let us pray] that your fair faith may be glorified in an abundance of the fruits of mercy, that he may keep your foot from the stumbling blocks of sins and from every oppressing pain, and that he may fill you with the abundance of his help at all times. For you, [let us pray] that the guilty man who seemed to you to be such may turn from his single [?] misery to the mercies of repentance, be found worthy of salvation by grace, and obtain the openness of face that is hoped for. For if so it happens, blessed be the mercy of our Lord, who visits the suffering by his grace even when we do not ask or think of it. Hope, then, in the Lord, O beloved of God, and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the earth. Turn the hope of everyone toward him, and you will live.

Do not look for the likenesses of the excellent among the weak, if those who seemed to you such are really so. Nor be offended when you do not find them. Nor let a lie creep in on you through hearsay, so that you imagine excellence in people far away, as has now happened to you. For we are all human beings and children of the earth, of scattered dust and molded of passions; and all alike fall short of the glory of God. Yet it is good to be zealous for good things; it is good to speak of good things; it is better still to do good things. Yet blessed is the one whose iniquity is forgiven and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord does not reckon his sin, and in whose heart there is no deceit. Let us all, then, desire this blessedness by grace, so that by grace we may be made worthy of it, through the grace of our good and merciful God forever. Amen.

The poor church of the Ninevites greets your love; it has received your greeting by letter, especially those who are closer to our Lord, to whom you particularly sent the gift of peace. May the greeting of its lowly ones return to all those who fear God with you; and pray for me. Peace.
29. Ishoyahb to John my brother: peace in our Lord.

Desire is called by everyone the wellspring of thought, the thing that longs to meet its beloved. Through so many years [our desires] have worn themselves out on you in vain, and now it has [subsided?], and we no longer go on feeling it, since it rests on a hope that is never fulfilled. Nor should you go on sending us empty promises of a visit that has not been [made good?]. Give it its own time, and be at peace. And pray for me from
afar, as it is good for you to do. And write to tell me about your needs, and be well. Peace.
30. Ishoyahb to Narsai and to Maremmeh my brothers: peace in our Lord.

That you come under pressure of persuasion to remember your brother, my brothers, and send greetings under compulsion to a weak man who is such a one to you, is a reproach and a great shame. It came about from no other quarter than the death of a love that does not die, a love for which we were once thought to be above everyone. For it has not died, as you will no doubt say; it has not died, but it is sick and sorely choking: in one member from the passion of offence, in another from the pain of contempt. Yet blessed be the mercy of our Lord, who from time to time renews in us the breath of the fragrance of its kinship, like a resurrection, as he has now moved your excellence to remember by letter one who had been forgotten through distance, even if the wording of it was used in a strange manner. Even this was said out of sickness, for forgetfulness is akin to sickness, and both belong to a suffering soul. Yet even so, and for this alone, I thank the goodness of our Lord, that he has in every way kept for us a remnant of acknowledgment across long memories. I pray too that the wealth in which many once took pride may not sink again and be diminished further than this.

But how are you, then? And again, how are you? I wanted to know. May our Lord grant in his mercies that you be as it is right for you to be. And you too, pray for me, that I may be worthy of mercies and find the grace of repentance
that serves to heal my pains, and that I may see you in peace as the Lord wills. Peace.
31. To the chaste and beloved of God, the holy priest Mar Sabrisho the bishop: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

A little from the pressure of your trial, and a little from the sight of the [?] garment of the many-colored head, O beloved of God, when they were joined to one another [?]. By the grace of God they prepared the sight of your love for my weakness. And from the [?] of the length of time, I have good memories of you on my part every day. I hope also to think of your affairs with a good conscience. Above all, when the son of your love, my brother Mar Sergius the priest and teacher, came to me, he eased my longing a little with the good news of your health. And I long to see you through him, as far as that is possible, by a greeting of peace. I beseech you to remember me in prayer before God at the times of the sacrifice which you offer before him on behalf of all, that I may be able to spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. And when you find someone coming to the region of Assyria, write to tell me of your health, so that I may rejoice. And be well. Peace.
32. To the chosen of God, Mar Samuel the priest: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

"Blessed is the man who takes up the yoke of Christ from his youth," says the prophet of God; "he sits alone and is silent, because he has taken his yoke upon himself." For this is the work of righteousness, peace, as he says; and its service

of righteousness, quietness and hope forever. Therefore whoever is such is blessed in his work. Rejoice, then, in your hope, chaste one, and strive in the good contest of excellence that you have taken up, so that you may attain the eternal life to which you were called. And pray for my weakness, I ask you, that I may be worthy of the grace of repentance and find mercy before our Lord on the day of his revelation. I will see you soon, when God wills. But before that, remember me every day and do not forget. Peace.
33. To my honored beloved, Mar John the priest:

Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

One adornment of bodily beings is speech; one adornment of speaking beings is wisdom; one adornment of the wise is love. All three come from the gift of God's goodness: the first by nature, the second by teaching, the third by the spiritual law. Therefore whoever is well perfected in this should be placed in the good that perfects. It is good also for whoever [holds to] this to hold to the excellent choice. Since I hold the one I hold, as I hold him, the perfection of the choice has always followed upon the choice, as it does now. For I received through our brother Sergius the teacher the greeting of your love, sweet in its fragrance, and you gladdened me with the good news of your health, as was fitting, though not in writing, as would have been fitting. And rejoicing, I thanked our Lord. May it please you, then, always to do toward me what befits your closeness to me, and do not refrain from praying for me, that I may be able to spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. Be well, and abound in love, which is an excellent possession for you. Peace.
34. To the all-holy, our father, the holy Mar Catholicos-Patriarch: your son Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

It befits excellence, our father, to excel in everything. So it is now: as is your custom, you were moved by the zeal of tender love toward my lowliness, and showed it in an abundance of remembrances. With five letters, as I have learned, you extended the fullness of joy to a weak man within a short time. Although they did not all reach me, because of the obstacles that arose, I was still amply granted cause to rejoice, learning how abundant is your paternity's care for me. I learned more about your affairs, as far as possible, from our brother Mar Ishoyahb the teacher. And I thank our Lord for everything, praying that you may be further strengthened in our Lord, for his glory and the glory of the community. For we have been shaken a little, but not utterly abandoned; and we can say, by way of comparison, that we are troubled but not forsaken. For the goodness of the merciful God still guides my weakness beyond what my sins deserve. And I am crushed by a conscience wrung by daily shame. I beseech your paternity, then, to pray that I may be delivered from the danger of body and soul, kept in the purity that is fitting, and spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. Peace.
35. Ishoyahb to Hormizd my beloved:

peace in our Lord.

If I had been the first, my brother, to greet you by letter, or again if I had answered you straight away after you wrote,

or again if after two or three [letters] I had shrunk from the confidence that was hoped for and held back from [?], then your glory would have been less, and my joy less as well. But now that what has happened has happened, and you have done what you have done, abundant glory is yours and complete joy is mine, both in their fitting distinction. Therefore, my brother, always outdo me in such things, and I rejoice. Do not tire of supplying such gifts to me and to all who love you, even if repayment of this praiseworthy debt falls short on our side. May the God of peace be with you and guide you without stumbling in all things. And pray for me too, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. Peace.
36. To the chaste and beloved of God, our honored brother Mar Elahzekha, priest and teacher: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

As for you, beloved of God, the pressure of daily obstacles has not found you sparing [?] every day toward that turning aside which made those who strayed from the victorious stations of your love wander toward the weariness [?] of my error. And so, in the very abyss of distance, in the very storm of confusion, in the very waves of afflictions, you have conformed yourself, with freedom of mind, to the claims of spiritual love. Twice you have sent a praiseworthy visit, with a greeting of peace, to the weak man that I am. And with great zeal you yourself took up the honored kindness of making the first approach. But for me, weak as I am, the mere gust of the world's trials is enough to drive me many times from

remembering the afflicted, and at times to keep me from the beauty of visiting that the spiritual law requires of the claims of love. Yet it was not so in what has now happened. For the violence of such obstacles was not enough, I think, beyond a mere outward distance, to dissipate the zealous and fervent meeting which the spiritual law seeks for its perfect use in your God-loving soul. That [weariness], indeed, you thrust aside on my part from the toils of afflictions with the help of God. And the constraint that kept me at a distance, as if bound in fetters of affliction, from turning from the place of my dwelling, has been softened by a few words. But through the openness of the trustworthy bearers, which came about in every way, I have been outdone, as I have been outdone up to now. Now, however, that I have read two letters, I in turn outdo the love that came first by the debt of my thanks. And I give blessing to your God-loving soul, as I weigh the occasion of your letter against love alone.

But I did not like the praiseworthy elegance in it, by which many pass over into the pitfalls of beauty through the habit of pleasure, and after them the snares of an afflicted conscience lie in wait, unless that too has been corrupted by the disease of insensibility. It is good, I think, for a free man moved by love to reveal himself to his beloved with domestic boldness and complete confidence. Let us then have the likeness of the blessed ones, who, moved purely by the spirit of love, left behind spiritual models of graceful correspondence as the inheritance of their labors, that by them all of us may be taught. And may the help of God bring us to the likeness of their excellence, in his grace and his mercies forever. Amen.

As for what you wrote to me,

my brother, groaning over the honor of high offices: do not marvel at the matter, for one higher than the high keeps watch, as it is written. But you, hope in the Lord and keep his way, and do the work of an evangelist, for this is your post. For with humble weeping it swallows up the proud dust, and the rod of humility subdues the insolence of the boastful. And if not with these, then with their own weapons; for one passion may well conquer another, as the saying goes. And if neither this way nor that, hope in humility that you may be worthy of the blessings that are written. And God keep you from all evil. Peace.
37. To the all-holy, our father, the holy Mar Catholicos-Patriarch: your son Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

The zeal of your paternity's love for the need of my weakness has grown very strong, our [?] father, and amid my idleness it has proved worthy of wonder. Neither the force of the affliction of the times nor all the things that are able to hinder the course of excellent perfections could keep your paternity's eagerness from brooding at every hour over the members of grace, which we all were appointed to be, and over me more than the others, who am all of this in weakness, as everyone well knows. For now again I have received the warmth of your paternity's love in a letter of peace, and I embraced its name in peace of spirit, and I thank your paternity's mercies with a humble conscience. I pray and long at every hour that soon the longing of my feet may come to rest in meeting your paternity, God helping. But until I am found worthy of this,
may it be done by grace, as it has been until now. And always send the gift of prayer to my weakness, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. Peace.
38. To the chaste and beloved of God, our honored brother Mar Aba the bishop: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

I received your loving letter with amazement, O lover of God, and I gave thanks to our Lord for his providence toward you. The weight of the suffering had sadly dragged me down into the depths of discouragement as I remembered every danger that your piety passed through at the hands of the wicked. But I was greatly encouraged by the hope your endurance gives, and I turned to praising God. For in the violence of your afflictions I saw what your persecutors were aiming at: through you, as through a member of the body of the faith, they were inflicting suffering on the Lord of glory. Then I also saw the contest of your endurance: in a weak body you bore the harshness of torments with the courage of soul of the athletes. Your body did not give way, as it naturally would, before the severity of the sufferings by fleeing from death, and your soul was not shaken, as it naturally would be, by the long disturbances that came every day. Nor did you hold back from sharing in the sufferings of its turmoil [?] by removing yourself to some other place. Instead, with the steadfastness of your whole person, you bore all the violence of the wicked with a humble and long-suffering spirit: until what seemed to be standing fell; until you were abandoned even by the one who should have helped you; until your suffering, and the boldness of the wicked in their violence, reached their limit; until, grievous as it all was, God was pleased in his mercy to make the power of his might perfect in the weakness of your infirmity. Because of these things,

then, O our brother, you have drawn out of my thoughts the great mass of discouragement that was left in them, and turned the sadness of my thoughts into thanksgiving to God. With joy I call your soul blessed, O lover of God, because you were made worthy to share in sufferings for the sake of his truth at the beginning of the contest which, as I think, is about to come upon many. For the mystery of iniquity and the revelation of the wicked one are, it seems, beginning from now on to hasten forward. Many are to be chosen and tested and made white, as it is written. Blessed are you, then, if you have fought and been tested and been found true. Blessed are you too even if you are still standing in the contest. But more blessed still if you are also counted worthy of greater things than these. For whoever is faithful in a little is faithful also in much, as it is written. Rejoice, then, in your hope, O blessed one, and be renewed in the spirit of your faith, as befits you. For from now on you also have the boldness that comes from suffering, to ask in prayer for mercy and help for the church of God. Pray, then, for this humble church of ours too, and for all who take refuge in it, that together they may be pleased to share with you, zealously, in sufferings freely chosen. All who are under my care, baptized believers and unbaptized believers alike, beg you to repay them for the blessing of their greeting with the reward of prayer in spiritual love. And I ask you to pray for my infirmity as well, that I may be made worthy of the grace of repentance and find mercy before our Lord, and spend the rest of my days in a life that pleases the will of God. The end.
39. To our father, holy in every way and pious, Mar Catholicos Patriarch: your son Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

Until now, O our father, the hope of your coming here, and my own eagerness to come there, were in a way lightening the pain of exile for our common spirit. But now that time, in its hardness, has done away with both of these, the suffering is shared among us all, and the griefs grow every day. So it is now necessary, in the customary way, to make use of lines of writing once again to console what is within us, until the Lord turns and has mercy on us and lets the light of his salvation dawn in his grace. Even so, let your fatherhood give thanks for these things that concern my lowliness. For by God's grace I am still better off than my sins deserve: I find my daily bread and a little rest, and the service of the church of God is carried out in a moderate order. This, it seems, ran contrary to the course of the world, as though even Satan could not bear the situation. So, burning with his usual purpose, he suddenly stirred up armies against us and great disturbances. And we are about to keep a Passover that resembles our Lord's Passover in every respect: on the same day, at the same hour, in the same manner, and in the whole service of those who carry it out. In place of Herod and Pilate, the chiefs and rulers of our country; in place of the high priests of the Jews and the rulers with them, the heretics and the great men of our own people; in place of the guards and soldiers, in place of the swords and clubs, these swords and clubs; in place of horns and shouting, these horns and shouts; in place of Judas

the betrayer, a renowned and honoured chief among our clergy [?]. While the holy sacrament was still between his lips, he showed more eagerness than Judas. For we did not even wait to sing the hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives, as even Judas waited. Nor did he come upon us with a kiss, as Judas did, but with violence and a blockade. Up to this point our Passover resembled our Lord's in everything. From here on, however, ours went further. It differed in every respect from our Lord's Passover, that bodily and mystical one with Peter and his companions, in this: that our Lord, who had once held back the twelve legions of angels from the service of their zeal by his word to Cephas, now sent them openly for the salvation of our church. And he worked wonders that show forth the glory of his power, wonders whose glory a letter cannot hold. My plain tongue cannot even sketch an outline of their marvel in the spoken word. Let them be kept, then, for when we meet face to face and can tell them at length, if God helps us. But before I am made worthy of that, let your fatherhood rejoice in what has happened, for it is truly glorious, and give thanks for it to our Lord at all times. For by the greatness of his strength his enemies, the heretics, have cringed before him, as it is written. When the blow of the Lord broke the strength of their hope, they turned to the barbarian rulers whom our sins have set over us. And now they are threatening me with death by every means, a death they have shown to be easy enough to inflict and even to their advantage. There is much to fear from them, since they are desperate men. Yet the Spirit of God, in his customary wonder, is turning even the harshness of the barbarians little by little to gentleness toward us. The barbarians are being shamed by these men as they were shamed by Assyria. And there returns

to the divine power, from the mouths of discerning men, the praise that befits it. So I beseech your fatherhood to pray that I may be made worthy of the grace of repentance and find mercy before our Lord, and spend the rest of my days in a life that pleases the will of God. The end.
40. To our father, holy in every way and pious, Mar Catholicos Patriarch: your son Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

As for me, O our gentle father, my experience of what had happened before was enough to persuade me to despair of good news in anything we desire for the service of our calling under the law of spiritual love. From the outset I wanted to be excused from taking part in these contests. But your fatherhood's command, together with the request of the honoured brethren, compelled me to put what had already been tried to the test once more. For you supposed, as I too once supposed, that those whose will is in command can be turned away from evil habits. You both asked and commanded on this matter, and I obeyed. But our common hope did not succeed in the excellent things that were fitting, because the stubbornness of evil habits proved stronger than the persistence of those who do not change. These men have tasted the pleasure of easy authority and found that they never tire of contempt. So now it is inevitable that people fall into the same troubles again and again, that people be stirred up over the same matters again and again, and that your Beatitude be distressed over the same things again and again. For this reason I inform your fatherhood briefly of things that are hard to set out in brief. At this time two uncanonical bishops, Shemishoʿ and Narsai, gathered with our father, the humble [?] Mar Metropolitan

of ours. They were repaying him the debt of the uncanonical laying on of hands that he had earlier lent them, and so they joined him in doing what he wanted. They found a man who is, as they themselves say, simple and ignorant. They did not know what country he is from, or where he now lives, or even what his name is. They did not know what manners and customs he was brought up in, what his work and trade in the world is, whether he is counted among the ranks of the church, or whether he even belongs to the pure church of the orthodox at all. They did not know where he had come from or where he was going. On such a man as this they conferred the title of bishop, and sent him off wherever the wind might take him. Some of them say it was to Adurbadgan, but in truth no one knows where. So what has now happened has happened as a 'correction' of what had wrongly happened before. But I know that your fatherhood does not believe these things, and you do well not to believe them. For it is very hard to believe such folly [?] and senselessness of conduct of men who are supposed to be discerning. However, if the Lord wills and I live and am made worthy to meet your fatherhood together with them, I will tell you the whole exact story of these matters: what we wrote to one another and what we said to one another face to face, before the event, at the time, and afterward. That is, unless the present end comes first and forestalls my eagerness, as with these events. But before I am made worthy to meet your Beatitude, pray for my infirmity, that I may find mercy before our Lord. The end.
41. To the lover of God, our honoured brother Mar Moses the priest: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

Once again, stirred by memory, you were carried away toward the urgency of your habit, and now too you have made use of a full string of titles for my name. And not long after a delay of years, you heaped up in a letter a great many extravagant praises from the very start and sent it to me. Some of them belonged to Zaphenath-paneah the son of Rachel, whoever he may be; some to the son of Jesse, whoever he may be; some again to the son of Amram, whoever he may be; and others even to the son of Amittai, whoever he may be. And since even these were apparently not enough for you, you went on, by the measured comparisons of the poet's art [?], to lean toward the vagueness [?] of what revelation holds for the future, and you painted the portrait of a sort of Catholicos of fantasy. It would be enough to lead astray the foolish conscience of a weak man, if it happened upon such things. Then, after all this, you heaped up at the end of the letter the reason for writing it, to strengthen it, and with a great many words you dressed that too in the look of deep need. In this way, by the force of your entreaty, you gave a silent man a keen impulse toward your business. All this happened to you, I think, so that you would stir yourself to write to me a second time, because you had not taken due care earlier in reading what I wrote at the time in reply to your former letter. For I had already given you some gentle persuasion by way of moderation: that in such sufferings, good order requires that a free man be moved, one who, for the sake of the spiritual law, spiritually, or rather for the sake of brotherhood, takes up what a letter asks of him and fulfils it. Since, then, what was written earlier about this was not read by you, things are the same now as well. And

look, I too am reluctant to write about the same things over and over. Still, I understood from what you wrote, and from what I learned from others, that the blow of the bread shortage has reached you too. Because of it, the priestly people has endured much agitation of every kind, so that even begging has been turned the wrong way round, from those who were always well fed to the hungry of all generations. When I learned this, I suffered as was fitting. But I was not fully able to support the needs of the poor as justice demands. For the blow came to us too, as you know: that whole age which has brought you into unaccustomed need. It touched us lightly at first, then surrounded us heavily, and we still lie beneath it. It has driven us back toward our usual need through the multitude of demands that weigh on us [?], or that cannot be met at all. Yet I was moved a little by the spiritual law, a little by the entreaty of my brothers in need, and a little again by the distress of those who ask out of the depths of need. And so I divided the little bread I had acquired in various ways, as far as I could: some in money, some in kind, and some for the distress of the world. I did it according to the time, according to the person, and according to the yields of the villages. A share of it reached you too: in kind, bread for about ten days; in money, as much as would last about twenty days; by quantity, three asar [?]; by weight, the full load of your beast; by the common measure, thirty griwe; by kind, ten of wheat and twenty of barley; and in will and in full measure, all you need, if only I could. So accept what is given in deed for what it is, and do not despise what is given in will as if it were nothing. And if it should happen that your affairs turn from this when the flood of suffering [?] , be to us as
befits you. And if you are not in need in these matters, that is the grace of our Lord's mercy. Give thanks for his care over us every day. And you, pray for my lowliness, and farewell. The end.
42. To our father, honoured in every way and pious, Mar Cyriacus, bishop and metropolitan: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

It is good for a man, O our father, more than any other good, to have a little peace for the church of God when it is prospering. And it is good for the church of God, more than a great many other aids, to have a little harmony among God's priests, however small, when it springs rightly from love. For by the first, that is, by the welfare of the church, the stability of the world is maintained with the help of the divine mercies. And by the second, that is, by priestly harmony, the stability of God's glory triumphs in the thanksgiving of eager tongues. So it has happened now. Rightly, like a flame growing in strength, your fatherhood's honour has been moved toward my humble lowliness with the sweetness of the fragrance of God's glory, that which, as the whole world and the writings of the Spirit say, is and is called love. I do not know on what wings it flew so lightly, as on breezes, and sprinkled the powers of its sweetness over the many who stood in the way. Some of them it turned toward the word of custom, others toward thanksgiving for discernment. And others, who had been tried by the opposition of circumstances and by the failure of their requests, it turned toward abundant hope. Then, as though they had found an opportunity of help for their good desire, they seized on the praised freedom my lowliness enjoys with your fatherhood, which God has provided out of love

and out of the fullness of your wisdom. And so, ahead of the many others who are already about to come, so that they may now see how my lowliness succeeds with your fatherhood, they came forward to approach your love through me. They are sons of your fatherhood's flocks and brothers of mine and of us all: those in the eastern part of your pasture, whose fold reaches as far as Balad. They graze pleasantly on the edges of the desert and rest in perfect peace by the waters of Eden that flow from the source which goes toward Assyria. Many times things have turned out well for them. Once, Joseph the victorious dwelt in the mother of cities, which is now governed by your fatherhood's care. I mean Paul, that wonderful persuader of counsel and champion of the word of truth. And another time, a little while ago, indeed now, before our very eyes, it sent to the royal city and patriarchal throne an honoured adorner, whose excellent qualities even foreign mouths are compelled to proclaim. With things standing as I say, they took it as a sign that they would prosper. Now they have set the eyes of their thoughts on the man beloved of all, our honoured brother Mar Maruzan the bishop, and have asked that he be their support for this time. When their hope was not fulfilled as easily as they expected, they became discouraged and distressed. Then they found what seemed a hope, one close at hand: that because of the warmth of your fatherhood's love toward me, I would be able to do this. They made me hopeful, and begged me with many supplications to persuade your fatherhood, some of them by coming to me in person, and all of them by a letter of request. Overcome by the fervour of my feelings and relying on your fatherhood's readiness toward me, I hastened to serve the matter according to the desire of these children, and to persuade your fatherhood as far as I can, though not

as is fitting. For I had thought that I would stand before you in person about this and do whatever the matter required. But it is not possible to do so openly, as would have been good; it is only possible to see you by letter, as time permits. So I ask you, O honoured father, may it please your love. Fulfil your children's request with good will, and give rest to my lowliness too. I am not saying, 'Praise me for this.' And do not be troubled at all over this, a deed that is fair and praiseworthy in everyone's eyes. Here the divine choice has already come before the human choice, and what do we have to add of our own? If there is something divine in an illness, as the physicians say, or rather, if matters are subject to human will, then it is easy, I think, to follow their lead. Perhaps your fatherhood is held back by concern for propriety of this kind: that the dignity of the metropolitan see has its rank, and it is not fitting for it to be lessened by a small place. If so, the difficulty is easily resolved on every side. To pass over many other points, take this one alone: such a request does not diminish the perfection of the person's own soul [?]. On the contrary, it grows greater when it stoops to small things. Nor does granting the request diminish the gift for the one who gives it. It is made greater still when it turns the request into a desire fulfilled. Besides, it is also good for your fatherhood's honour that your sons should become fathers, and that metropolitans of others should be counted among the least of your disciples. And if that is not the reason, but rather some insensitivity, as it were, on the part of the person is put forward as the reason for refusing, which of these is it fitting to put forward? And how could we persuade, on this point, the many peoples and renowned cities in which the testimony to this man's chastity is proclaimed in many tongues?

I say this as well. Suppose this man is not as excellent as all who know him say, but is otherwise in the sight of God, while he is well regarded among men, and all this is fittingly said of him by everyone who knows him. Such a deficiency does no harm to people in any way, since it is entirely hidden from them. Nor do I think it easy for all men to begin thinking ill now of one who in many trials has already received testimony to his uprightness. And again, suppose it is not in such matters but in the kind of deficiencies that are found in all of us. If your fatherhood's refusal looks to these and blocks this arrangement, who then will escape danger? Who can say, 'I have made my heart clean, I am purified from my sins'? Or whose hidden conscience about his sins does not leap up against his openness of face? I for my part sincerely reproach myself: I am worthy of neither heaven nor earth. I have never washed my hands in purity and gone around the altar of the Lord. And from now on I confess against myself that I am not even worthy of the divine mercies. I am a wretched man, brought low by sufferings. Yet I am greatly upheld by God's goodness. Yet the church of God too looks on me with a compassionate eye. Yet neither excellent men nor even those godly ones despise my lowliness. For all the knowledge of the wise, it seems, knows how to bear the deficiencies of others more than its own. And this is how all of us must live with one another and toward the church of God. And I think, O honoured father, that since you are able to show wisdom in greater things than these, you are bound to set things right even more than those who are clever about them. It is neither profitable, then, nor

advantageous for the matter to change from the firmness of persuasion into an occasion of stumbling. For how could it not change, especially through hasty tongues? They will at once give the matter the name of agitation, that is, envy, and trouble you and us and the whole common mind. Already, even outside the laws of the church, a stumbling block is being spread. And who can live? Or who would not be forced to give up the ghost every day, if he has a conscience that is moved by shame? Yes, my father, let me find mercy before you. Receive the entreaty of my lowliness with a fatherly heart. By the power of your wisdom provide an excellent fulfilment for the matter at hand. Give rest to the desire of your sons in their fair request. Help your little flock [?] in a way that brings settled order. And grant my lowliness too the confidence [?] that comes from having an entreaty accepted, so that in whatever may happen I may rely on this present freedom and approach you with trust. And when, with God's help, I have rightly decided, I will also help others from your fatherhood, and spread your fatherhood's honour among others, ahead of the [?] that are to come in this present matter. For he who was twice entrusted with victory [?] for two mother-cities is fully able, by God's grace and with your fatherhood's help, to govern without fault this small and gentle pasture. In this way honours will increase, the church of God will have the order that befits it, and for my lowliness and for those who are eager for good, the reason to give thanks to the glory of God will grow. May he in his grace make your fatherhood's honour triumph in his church all the days of your life. Amen. The end.
43. To one who is faithful in truth and falls little short of the praise he deserves, our honoured and chosen chief, Mar Yazdin: Ishoyahb, peace in our Lord.

…that it is not for lack of zeal, nor again because of the turmoil of daily affairs, that my lowliness and your greatness have so far failed to meet each other, even if only through lines of writing. The length of the delay is plain already to you and to me, and also to those who are concerned about it. While I acquit you from the outset of such a fault, because the reasons are evident, I place myself under the guilt of having taken my ease. For it was right that, from the moment the adverse turn of affairs befell your honour at the hands of the priests of God, until the trouble reached the point of danger, to our grief and to the distress of the whole church of the Lord, I too, weak as I am in power of mind, should have run to the help of your soul and thrown a little water on the flame. If the matter called for healing, I would have taken my place among the ministers. And if it called for the labour of persuasion, reconciliation and full assistance, even then I would not have been counted as a stranger among those who are concerned for your honour, the goodness of your name and the growth of your virtues. Now, however, because of the adversities that have befallen us, the tangled turmoil of oppressive changes, and the great affliction that has sunk the whole world in the depths of despair, I too have been kept from what I was bound to do, both through slackness and because of the extraordinary afflictions that Satan has stirred up against me through the ministers of his will, the heretics who are enemies of God.

The letter of your love reached me, and from it breathed the fragrance of the love of true faith, sweet and pleasant. It roused [?] me, feeble and small of soul as I am, to the struggle. Indeed, zeal for the faith and love of orthodoxy become you on every side. They come from your father, whose faith, I think, fell little short of that of Peter and of Abraham. They come from your mother, who also did not lag far behind her partner in the greatness of her faith. And they come again from you yourself, since you have long been proven in that strength of conduct which is equal to the testing of affairs such as these. You did well, then, to come forward to my help in the struggle that Satan has thrust upon me through the wicked who serve his wiles. May your strength grow greatly, with the help of God to strengthen you. Add greater zeal every day, until it reaches an excellent fulfilment that moves all who fear God everywhere to give thanks to God. To set down in a letter the nature of affairs here would run to excessive length: the audacity of the wicked, how the movement of their madness began, who dared to follow after us, how they now trouble the rulers and the people of the land every day and keep up a constant oppression, and what I in my turn, under pressure, have thought of doing, whether by going to the rulers or by sending to them, and everything of that kind. So, to inform you of all of it, I have sent ahead to you our honoured brother Mar Ḥnanishoʿ, the head of the monastery, so that you may hear from him what is needed, and also do what is needed. After this, I beg you by the mercies of God not to change the course of your life by anything that is thought contrary to the fear of our Lord. Give no opening to the enemies

of the Lord to put a stain on your honour, as on an honoured member of the body of our Lord. Let not the heat of your passion become a heartbreak to us, nor let the taunting of the enemies be lodged in it every day like a tormenting thorn. Yes, my brother, give rest to my love in Christ. Turn to your conscience with spiritual grief. Look a little at what is near, and consider a little what is far off. Let your father in the flesh be your model of virtue, he whose great faith God displayed in his very deeds, and whose zeal in the fear of God is remembered and celebrated on the lips of many. Why, then, as in his day, are the compassionate feet of the priests of God not constantly in the courts of your house? Why is your table not sanctified every day by the faithful blessings of the saints of our Lord? Why is your dwelling not always blessed by the pure prayers of the ministers of the Lord? And to speak more loftily still: why are not all who need correction and seek repentance everywhere provided for and set in order in you and by you? For all these things your eyes and the eyes of all of us saw, in repentance and in the fear of our Lord, in that blessed man whose substance, house and honour you have inherited. From the Lord came all goodness; but from you, I do not know what. I beg you, therefore, our brother: remember the goodness of our Lord. Remember the afflictions that brought you near to death, those many times when he turned you back from the depth of despair of the flesh to a life you had not hoped for. Remember all the peril of the sufferings by which man's little life is found choked in the vicissitudes of trials and is exchanged for natural death in the bitterness of adversity. Remember, then, that we are dust, and that our days on earth are like a breath. We are like water poured out on the ground, which cannot be gathered up.

I know, our brother, I know that you are a strong-hearted man, a person without fear, who feels sufferings but lightly. From this it also comes about that you despise sins as you despise those who rebuke you, as it is written: Lack of fear and lack of shame make sins firm. Who then is Paul, or who is Apollos, that you are angry with them? Is it as enemies that they preach the truth to you? Or are they cunning men who rob you by deceit? Was not the one who has long been the priest of your city your tutor, or rather your foster-brother? Did he not hold unfeigned love toward you and your whole father's house, in justice? Did you not formerly bestow good pledges on him, on his people and on his monastery? Should he then repay you evil for good? Cursed, according to Scripture, is the one who does so. And he truly would have repaid evil had he been negligent and kept silent about your intention at a time when the stumbling caused by your passion had spilled over onto the church of our Lord as well. He would have been an enemy if he had not spent all the strength he had in the struggle for your correction. Now that he has done what he was bound to do and fulfilled the spiritual law out of human love, is he to be thought your enemy because he preached the truth to you? But you say: I have already been wronged for no reason, and I am innocent in my own eyes and before God. Very well. Why, then, do you not establish your innocence openly, to the conscience of the priest who loves you and of all the saints of our Lord? For this is what they all seek, and pray that they may find: to gain you as a free son, clear of blame. But if your conscience is not pure before God in the matter for which his priests rebuke you, why are you angry with the priests? Why do you despise your own correction? Or why do you revile

those who rebuke you, thinking that you are harming them by this? For it is plain where the harm will remain. And if it is neither the one nor the other, but you are already despising and stopping your ears, spurning and kicking against the healing remedies of the Christian life and the humbling remedies that go with them, with a conscience, as it were, shaken and hiding itself in the darkness of insensibility, then from now on you are in need of the abundant prayer of the saints, lest, God forbid, you incline even to this fall, which may God not allow to happen. Let not the grief of your inclining and the evil of your loss become the breaking of our people and the joy of our enemies. Let not those who hate you say, "Aha, aha, our eye has seen it!" But may the Lord save, the Lord deliver, the Lord help, the Lord have mercy, the Lord pity, the Lord turn you back, the Lord act. May the Lord raise [?] you from the dust of sins and lift you from the dunghill of sufferings. May the Lord give a new heart and a new spirit; may the Lord give strength and might to his servant. Blessed be God! Persevere in prayer. Do not let the service of the Lord slip away from you. Receive the reading of the Scriptures of the Spirit with the delight of discernment. Whenever the divine mysteries are consecrated, cast yourself on your face on the ground. Let your heart ache and let your tears run down. Take up the cry of the tax collector many times and without ceasing, saying: "God, have mercy on me, a sinner." When your heart is moved in the groanings of prayer, call on the Lord, and he will open the eyes of your understanding, so that you may know how you stand and what you ought to do. When you know, take care to correct yourself. When you are corrected, love those who were concerned for you. When you love them, honour them as priests of God and rejoice with them. And in the fellowship of joy, praise together with them

God who has strengthened you. Give also to my lowliness and to the whole holy church cause for thanksgiving and gratitude, to the praise of the merciful God, who wills that all people should live and turn to the knowledge of the truth and to the life of righteousness. May he by his grace strengthen you to do his will always, all the days of your life. Amen. It is finished.
44. To the one honoured in all things, our holy father Mar Gabriel, bishop and metropolitan. Ishoʿyahb, in our Lord, greeting.

That the lot of his brood [?] has fallen to dwell near the nest of Satan, our father, where he hatches the offspring of vipers in every wilderness and finds in them destroying worms for the ruin of the life of all men, you are already persuaded, as of something plain to everyone. But how, whenever they find occasion in the disturbance and distress of the world, they are nourished and strengthened as if by a foul temper of the air, and creep quickly to harm weak people: this alone we who, according to the word of God to the prophet, have fallen to dwell among scorpions, or rather, as I said, among nests of vipers, must foresee and perceive. Therefore the evil prospect of the attack of the wicked, which I see as from a nearby watchtower, compels me to proclaim it far and wide, so that each person may be moved to take care of his life as far as his strength allows. For there has come upon the world, our father, what God has fixed [?], the end of ends, as you know. It has already come and taken hold of everything: the rebellion spoken of beforehand by the Spirit of God, which must come with the revelation of Satan. Or else it is near

at hand. Or rather, it has already begun to take effect in deeds: that saying, "When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?" Leaving aside the many other things, which I, in my smallness of soul, ponder feebly, this one alone, about which I have been compelled even to write, I make known briefly to your holiness. These wicked men and blasphemers of whom I speak have been carried away by the madness of their insanity on a satanic hope, and have found an opportunity for their success through evident causes. The first is the ready compliance [?] of the present rulers toward those who approach them with plates of silver and gilded persuasions. The second is the large number of evil helpers who formerly belonged to their heresy and are now counted among those in power. The third, again, is the favour and success of the merchants before the chiefs and rulers there. And the fourth, along with these, is the working of Satan, who is busy in the children of disobedience, those who did not believe in the love of the truth by which they would live. And so they went as they went and approached as they know how. They spoke no word of wisdom, offered no persuasion of understanding, showed no proof of belonging to the household of our Lord, and were not able to do even one of the things that are fitting and reasonable for an audience before rulers. Yet they obtained the fulfilment of their desire and turned to troubling us. They also found the local governor helping them fully. They went out to the dunghill before the gate of our city, being themselves the dunghill of the church, and made themselves a house of mockery and contempt under the name of a church, near the meeting place of all those who are

accustomed to go there to relieve nature. From there they stir up pretexts for disturbance every day, and above all through the constant blasphemies that they bark every day with insolent mouths against the church of God. And those who are honoured among our people are old offspring of their heresy; they belong to them, and are theirs both by nature and by choice. And the one who appears to be, as it were, the head of them all, and whom the times have also greatly prospered, was born of an orthodox Christian father and a heretical Christian mother. He began on his mother's side, walked a little on his father's, and after that was carried off to the latest kind of paganism, which is evident among the apostates [?]. After that, again, from this wavering paganism he went over to fellowship with the heretics. When he was pressed by worldly shame, as if by a prick of conscience, he turned a little toward the church of God, until the fear of death and the anger of the rulers made him turn aside. Now he goes about like a dog returning to its vomit, back to the root of bitterness that sprang up in him through his mother. He has turned to the madness of craftiness, and for those eager for wickedness he is a pillar of confidence and one who emboldens [?] those who are ashamed. Because of this they exalt themselves, are puffed up and are hard to bear, as it is written: I saw the wicked boasting and lifting themselves up like the trees of the forest. Our people, however, are poor in strength and needy in wealth, and altogether empty of power and of worldly knowledge. Yet there is in them, by the help of God, the zeal of true faith. They are deeply grieved and astonished at the evil sight of the defiled sign that Satan has set at the gate of their city. And many times they are also inflamed by the madness of zeal to rush into the danger of death, in things that are against the times

as they are. But it seemed to me helpful to calm the people who love the faith from the fury of their agitation by the customary admonition, and for me myself to refrain from going before the rulers of the time, since I am bearing a bodily sickness that is not much less than suffering and distress of soul. And now, with the help of God, I have begun the resistance, persuaded that I must take my stand in the middle of the merchant town as in a theatre of the wicked. Apart from the one who is like a thorn [?] in the middle, who is already found there, many of those with him are also opposed to me and are helpers of the wicked. But it lies in the hands of God, as it is written: all goodness, that he may abound in his works [?]. For even if, because of the unworthiness of my weakness, he should wish to let his truth be despised in the words of those who are under the attack of his persecutors, even so the small labour I spend for the cause of his truth will not be without profit to me, the sinner. And thanks be to his mercy toward me in all things. But if he does the better thing and gives the truth of his faith the glory it deserves in this time, which is, as it were, the forsakenness of the world, then from now on, through the agreement of many, thanksgiving will abound to the glory of his name at all times. If, then, your fatherly wisdom, honoured father, or the zeal of the people who love Christ, whose gentle faith has been nurtured on the foundations of God's goodness, has any help to give, whether of sensible counsel, or support of bodily labour, or anything else that is seen to bear on this present struggle, do it diligently, as befits your excellence above all, in everything that makes the beauty of Christians prevail in the glory that befits it. But if time hinders you from such things with its adversities, then suffer with us on our behalf, especially in the church of God,

and pray for us in humility of heart, that God may open to us a door for the word, to restore to the truth of his faith the glory that is due to it, and that he may return us in peace to the service of our calling, without oppression and without harm from the wicked. So that you may know how things stand with us and what they have intended to do, I am sending to you our honoured brother Mar Ḥnanishoʿ, the head of the monastery. Receive him in the Lord, as you know how, and send him off in peace and quickly, so that he may soon come to me, wherever the merciful God is pleased in his grace to make known to us. Let the greeting of my lowliness be given by the hands of your fatherhood to all the sons of your fatherhood, my beloved brothers, both those of the community and those within it. And pray for me, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. It is finished.
45. To the lovers of God, my beloved brothers, the chaste clergy and the faithful people in the city of Balad. Ishoʿyahb, in our Lord, greeting.

I have read what you wrote to me, my brothers, and I thanked our Lord for your zeal in the fear of God. But I was greatly shaken with astonishment and perplexity when I suddenly came upon joy at what had happened. For the labour of your present zeal is not a small thing, as it may appear: to secure for yourselves a spiritual guardian at a time of the world's faithlessness. Yet no less great is the simplicity shown in matters that hold to the order of succession from the ancient ways: on the one side, as far as the simplicity of the request; on the other, as far as the simplicity of the obedience of the whole community, or rather of the heads of the community. Therefore, my beloved, until the outcome

of these things, I hold both joy and sorrow over the zeal of your love. For I do not yet know how what has newly been done at your hands will be judged, and whether justly, by the head of the church's administration or by the administrators of the community. This is truly something new. How was it found among the people of Balad? Who persuaded them that it was possible, a thing that has never been tried among men? Or from where did they come to such a meeting with one another: a city in need of a bishop and a bishop in need of a city, a people that approves the person and a person who is pleased with the people, and all of this so that they run to one another out of zeal? When anyone considers these things, he is poured out in perplexity of thought, both as to how the affair will be shown and as to its final outcome, as I said. Caution, then, is called for in everything. Let it be so that the people do not regret what they did, the person does not suffer for his obedience, the metropolitan is not much moved to be troubled with anyone or troubled at what has happened, and the report of what you have done is not carried to our father the Mar Patriarch by others, in a change of administration. Rather, repay each one diligently what is due to him: honour to whom honour, love to whom love, obedience to whom obedience, persuasion to whom persuasion. And to our father the Mar Patriarch, before everything, a report of what has happened. The faults of the affair and also its merits are known in part, and to put it briefly, they are these. Fitting is the bishop whom you chose. Fitting also the people who chose him. Fitting the fullness of the election, which was established by the whole people, and together with the people by strangers as well. Fitting too

the zeal of your fervour, that you did not disdain to bring yourselves a spiritual establishment at this time, when repentance is despised by many. Fitting also the great labour you spent in persuading the metropolitan, or in petitioning those who could persuade him. But it is not fitting, I think, my brother, that out of the fervour of zeal you should seize such affairs into your own authority. Nor is it fitting that anyone, in the simplicity, as it were, of love of the good, should despise the ecclesiastical order that has been followed canonically through the traditions of old, and that requires a right agreement from all the ranks of the church. If, then, my brothers, it is easy to heal the stumbling that has come, or is coming, upon the fathers of the community from the unfittingness of such a thing, do diligently and without disdain whatever seems useful to you. For I suppose that you thought about these matters before you began to act. And just as you intended, so complete it. May our Lord open before you the door of his peace everywhere, and strengthen you with the spirit of his wisdom to heal the matters [?] that need it. May the power of your persuasion, with the help of God, lead to the agreement, unity and love of your people toward your metropolitan and all the fathers of the community. May the throne of your city be rightly set in order, and may the beloved priest whom you chose sit on it in truth, in the tabernacle of the Lord. May the sweet spirit of the Lord guide him in the way of life, to follow justice, to hasten after righteousness, and to show holy mercy toward the debts of the people for length of years. May the Lord rejoice in his works, and may the soul of the people exult in him. May his strength increase in good works, may the people be blessed by his prayer, may the peace of your city be firmly established, and may the harmony of love increase among all the ranks of your church. And may the right hand of God's help keep you
from all harm every day. May you be strengthened and sanctified to keep his commandments always, all the days of your life. Amen. It is finished.

As it seems to me, our brother, and as is pleasing to all who fear God, though you also give your approval, this is the only way it is right to write to you: To the chaste and God-loving, our honoured brother Mar So-and-so. Ishoʿyahb, in our Lord, greeting. I beg you, our brother, keep away from this labour that has been laid upon you, and spare yourself from the tongues of everyone. Serve God rather in a humble spirit, mindful that the quiet life, which all the saints praise, is helpful. Pray for the peace of the world and the peace of the holy church. Pray also for me, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. But since the time demands it, and the cause calls, and your holiness has undertaken to bear it, I am compelled to write as follows: To him who has sanctified the senses of his body by spiritual labours, so that through him the light of hidden things dawns upon the dark world; who in spirit serves the needs of the community through the lamp of his bright mind; who from the gold of his lips holds out to every soul victorious salvation in all times of affliction; who supplies the nourishment of peace and the sweetness of rest to the crushed hearts of needy people; and who in all things resembles the one whom the saving word set as a model for the perfect to follow. Nazirite of truth and strict humility, perfect model of the ways of the Spirit, our honoured master Mar So-and-so. The least of all and weakest of all, Ishoʿyahb the sinner, who bears the name and serves

the monastic habit with a wretched conscience, in need of mercy at every hour to find the hopes of grace from the Lord of all: in him, our Lord, the fountain of peace, may peace increase to you at every hour. That the abundance of the beauty of deeds surpasses the praise of words, or prevails over praises, the conscience of many is enough to persuade. Indeed, to recall them is no less [a tribute] than their success, and even than the inability [to praise them]: in the one case as far as the pressure of need, in the other as far as the witness of the mind. So I did not think it necessary [to praise you], lest one who is modest [?] should suffer in praises as if from reproaches. For how could we not suffer if poverty of persuasion should hinder [?] the glorification of those who testify? And especially in the case of one who, even at the beauty that appears within him, already sees the measure of his own smallness. Therefore let the glory that comes from God suffice for the praises of your honour, O chaste one, carried along with the humility that runs with it. Now I urge you only on that matter on which I am compelled to urge you. You know that I have been appointed to be the servant and minister of this poor people of Nineveh, and for all the adverse sufferings that befall them the service of their relief is required of me. Along with all the others they had [?] a good guardian and a wise helper, the honoured Mar So-and-so, on whose account they lived in abundant peace. Many benefits also came to our country through his bearing of the burden, and especially to the churches and the monasteries and to our whole order, as you yourself know especially well. But the times have begrudged us our rest and snatched the helpful man away from us. And amid a multitude of dangers we are bound to be distressed, if God should keep him [from us] [?], as indeed we have already begun to suffer.

Therefore I urge you, through the hands of this poor people whose service I am bound to, to write about these matters to the one who holds authority and governs the community, that he may return this man, So-and-so, to us. You are able, if you wish, to help us with power, and so that this request of yours may turn without hindrance to the relief of us all, and with us of all our region. Do not withhold, then, the gift of help from the poor people who call upon you, O lover of God. Do it in your accustomed way, and help the weak who ask. And together with your letter on this matter send a persuasive force sufficient to bring the request of the weak to a helpful fulfilment. Then we shall receive this governing man as from your hand. When you do this, you will purchase for us a dwelling of peace. And to the churches and monasteries and all the saints in them, so that they may be able without hindrance to carry out the service of the community in their customary prayer: they will help you in the struggle for the peace of the world, to the glory of the name of the Lord. May he in his goodness make your end victorious in the church, to the glory of his worshippers. Amen. It is finished.
47. To the one honoured in all things, our holy father Mar Cyriacus, bishop and metropolitan. Ishoʿyahb, in our Lord, greeting.

I received with joy the letter of your love, O God-loving father, and I gave thanks to our Lord for your health. But that you have been so greatly shaken by the combined turmoil of distressing changes caused me much suffering too. A little earlier I had already received the report of your hardship concerning the [?] abundant supply of figs and of necessities, which the goodness of your land used to give in plenty, as a delight, to the inhabitants of your city. And I was distressed, with only faint hope, about

these things: that need had fallen suddenly, like a brother, upon the priestly people, and that through the onset of the trials that came upon them, people had lost the [?] abundance of their livelihood. For the rich of Nisibis were an example to the districts of Athor: the [?] of the pampered belly, in whom the markets of Nisibis used to stir up every day a craving for the food of the well-born. How did it happen that something no one would have believed could happen came to pass? That the lady, a daughter of renown, faithful in every good thing, who sustained many thousands of people, should be unable to find relief for her needy in the time of distress, beside the hungry crowd that was driven out by the ruin of Athor [?]? While I was tossed about in such turmoil of thoughts, not long after I also received the letter of your paternity, by whose reading the report of the suffering was confirmed beyond doubt. From then on I have continued to mourn your sufferings. For sufferings of every kind are being prepared for us too. And I say, in its season, what was spoken by the holy and life-giving mouth: "If these things happen to the green wood, what then will happen to us, who are dry wood" both by nature and by will? Yet thanks be to the mercy of our Lord, for both the one and the other. Let your paternity pray, I beg, that we may have a conscience worthy to draw in the refreshment of the sweetness of God above us, so that both through all his favours and through his chastisement he may give us to dwell in the fruits of eternal life. May we all be counted worthy of them by the mercies of our God's grace. Amen. As for the help your love asked of me to complete your letter, I wished to give it abundantly, with the readiness of a whole conscience. But the narrowness of my capacity held back the breadth of my intention: the scantiness of the means that serve bodily needs, such as the times are, such as the house is, such as

our circumstances are. So I have sent your paternity, according to my means and my intention, a thousand kors of barley, by measure and quantity a hundred griws, as you wrote to me. If at some later time we should come to be in need of them, you may give us back the principal with interest and something more. But if God's goodness keeps us beyond such needs, let the great church of Nisibis be in our debt for a thousand kors of barley forever. And mixing still more cheerfulness into suffering, I will say this: I searched all the treasuries along with all the coffers to find some article or gift fit to answer the well-ordered peaceful greeting that your paternity sent to my lowliness, and I found nothing. As it is said, wherever it is said: "For the fruits of our fields and the produce of our rivers bring such wealth into our dwellings." That is to say, need. However, some days ago a sign of our Lord's will rained upon us a few dates from the lower country, and I have sent them to your paternity, a humble offering unworthy of your greatness. They are many in number, which is not much less than the filling of one small measure. Let your paternity therefore accept them as befits the gift, and pray for me. Ended.
48. To the weak sons of true believers and Christians of the truth: Qamishoʿ, Sanya, Babusa, Hahishoʿ, Isaac, Bar Sahde and Dadizad. Ishoʿyahb, the stranger, who by the grace of God serves the church

holy of the Ninevites: in God who holds all things, may all peace abound to you. Most fitting for the downfall of the world and the ruin of human life is the evil of the lack of faith, which you alone, before the rest of the lost, have now happened to suffer, O wretched men. For in you has already been fulfilled what our Lord said about the present times: "When the Son of Man comes, will he indeed find faith on the earth?" For now, by the evidence of your conduct, you cry out as with a voice in answer to the report of our Lord's word: there is no faith among us. How so? I heard it at first and did not want to believe it. Then I heard it again from someone who told it, and I was forced to accept it without doubt: that a demon flew upon you, one of those rebels on the mountain of Alpap, and in the likeness of a boor he fastened the bolt on the door of the chamber that bore for you the honoured name of the holy church in the fortress of Beth Babai, and he set on it the seals of his incantations and went away. And all of you were rolling about there like lifeless stones. Your mouths were stopped from speech and your limbs dried up from action, and not one among you was found who would even move his hand up to his eyes and sign the sign of the cross on his face, or on his heart, so that the help of God might come to you. Then you would have been able to wake from the slumber of mental blindness, and to see what a lowly, despicable, contemptible and ridiculous thing Satan is to you, in a single unclean raven that serves his wickedness. But you stayed, as they say, without movement, without feeling and without sensation, like

deaf idols. You could not even bring out the holy mysteries from there, as even weak men would, men who show the most feeble sluggishness over some necessity of their own affairs. Instead, like people who have no hope and no God in the world, you abandoned even the holy and life-giving mysteries under the seal of demons.
