And all of you went off to the house of the miseries of your sins, with a shame of face you did not even feel. Who then can weep for you as is due? Or who is able, by the strength of prayer, to set right the ruin of your fall? Or how could you not be reckoned wretched and fit for the lowest [?] of heart by every person who keeps the mind of a Christian? For me, O wretched and slumbering men, could it be believed of you that you feel the matter at all, and that Satan has not entirely destroyed all the insight of your discernment? This is the evidence of your faith, that is, of your faithlessness and your unmoved indifference over this deed, which deserves astonishment and lament. It seems to me the beginning of the fall of the many who, at the time of the coming of the Satan of the world, will lose their souls from the faith of the truth of true hope, through all the deceit of iniquity that comes about in those who are perishing, as it is written. I groan greatly and am in anguish, and I sink into the depth of despondency, especially when I bring to mind where and in whom the stumbling-block of sin has begun to come, namely in you. For some of you are by your very lineage sons of blessed bishops, and some of you are the new heirs of true believers and the good disciples of honoured priests. And now, by the slackness of your will, you have lost all the good name of your fathers. If it were possible for him to be awakened

now from the sleep of death, the blessed Bishop Shemʿon, in whose days these heretical tares sprang up in the field of Christ in this region, and who waged great struggles against them unto blood and death, until he completed his contest and handed on his throne, his rank, his house and his inheritance to the heirs of his family; if he were to come now and see the sons of his sons, some of whose sons and daughters are as an offering to the heretics, the ministers of Satan, while others despise the sacred things of Christians, like people who have lost their minds, and have become partners, companions, receivers, honourers, praisers and comforters of the heretics, at whose hands he endured trials, what would he think and feel! With what voice would he have gone in to his weak sons, who denied the good inheritance of his faith and surrendered to heretics! But the evidence of the suffering is plain to the discerning, even if that priestly mouth is now kept silent by death from rebuking the change in his sons. For it will rebuke them then, at the proper time, before the fearful judgment-seat of Christ our Lord. So too the blessed Bishop Qamishoʿ, who by the labours of his zeal put an end to the worship of idols among the loathsome people, and left the good inheritance of the true faith to the sons of his discipleship and to his sons in the flesh. So too all the faithful fathers of each one of you, who departed from bodily life with a good name and a pure faith, and left you the inheritance of their faith, their possessions, their honour, their authority and their leadership. And even now, with the weapon of prayer, they strengthen the hope that is set upon you before God, the Lord of all. Behold, there is preserved among you,

by the help of God and by the faith and prayer of your fathers, all the honour, leadership and authority of your district at this time, so that you cannot find in any of our circumstances even a pretext to excuse the slackness and negligence in which you live. When the judgment of God upon you is made ready at the proper time, let every person confess the righteousness of God, that his judgments are entirely upright. I, then, O weak men, since I suppose that from the great contempt in which you hold me you are already weary of the letter as soon as it is unrolled, and perhaps will not even let anyone else read it to you, for this reason I am weary of writing to you about this matter as I ought. Besides, I think that at this time you need prayer for your help more than a letter. First, may God help you by the mercies of his grace. And I too, sinful and wretched as I am, if the good hope of your fathers' faith is preserved among you, and if you are at all pained by what has happened or not, and I wait to say whether you have not entirely lost the good of Christians, I wished to test you in this, even if to others it may seem otherwise. Until you take upon your hearts, your tongues and your hands the zeal of faith in our Lord, and break those unclean seals that Satan set by the minister of his will on the door of your church, and show for it the diligence that is due for its building, its relief, its priesthood and its sanctity, as befits the church of God, you are not permitted by our Lord's word to enter any of the churches in any place or to share in the divine mysteries. And if

it should happen that, while you enter boldly, you say, or the heretics deceive you into saying, that what happened happened by command of the Arabs, it is not true at all. For the Hagarene Arabs do not help those who ascribe suffering and death to God, the Lord of all. And even if they did help them for some reason, you are able to inform the Hagarenes and persuade them about this matter, so that the obstacle in it may be removed for you. Act therefore, my brothers, in all things with wisdom. Give to Caesar what is Caesar's and to God what is God's. And may God most high, who reaches out all goodness with his hands to abound among those who fear him, perfect you in every good work to do his will at all times, all the days of your life. Amen. Ended.
49. To our father, honoured in all things, Mar Gabriel, the metropolitan bishop. Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord.

A little while ago, O our father, when we were shaken by the harassment of the wicked, we turned the faces of our thoughts toward you, though in fear, as toward the firm pillars of orthodoxy. And we were ready to do what that time permitted. We wrote and informed you in faithful trust. Not long after the turmoil of those events, but at the very beginning of our setting out, the mercy of God's goodness suddenly flowed upon us with a wonder beyond words, and it drove the harassment of the wicked away from us: some of them far off, and others into the [?] of their hiding-places. And it turned us, in amazement, straight

to thanksgiving, according to the [?] of our custom. Not only that, but we also have a firmer hope that the evident power of our Lord will in a short while overturn the boldness of the wicked from its height, just as it has already begun to suffer. Let your paternity therefore rejoice in these things and give thanks to our Lord for them as is right. And for what is to come, pray that, by God's goodness, it may receive abundant fulfilment, for the glory of the holy church and the joy of the faithful. It seemed good to me to send to your piety, along with this writing, the writing that I composed a little while ago in the midst of the winter of distresses, so that you may know more fully the wickedness of Satan's ministers, the wonderful help of God's power, and the slight change by which he suddenly revived us out of his incomprehensible mercy. Knowing more fully, you will marvel, and marvelling, you will give thanks and praise. And with all this, pray also for my weakness, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. Ended.
50. To the lovers of God, my beloved brothers, John the priest and archdeacon, and Taʿi, head of the believers of Erbil, and all those with them who wrote to me. Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord.

I received and read what you wrote to me, and I gave thanks to our Lord for your zeal in good love and for the proof of your affection toward my lowliness. Yet the conscience of my lowliness does not consent to what some of you, as you say, have judged [?] to be expedient. For by what reasoning, if one examines it well, can such

a change be of help at this time? Either a person is moved to change for the hope of spiritual gains, or out of desire for bodily life and the other things that are arranged for human living in greater prosperity. Worshipping the goodness of our Lord, I confess that I have a moderate measure of these things here, and the grace of God has not neglected my lowliness so far that I should be swayed by the hope of the abundance of the age, things that are said to be found in other places. Nor should one let go of the advantage of his labour; the measured orders established with long diligence; the exchange of good customs acquired for training; the perseverance in the long contest against heretics and pagans; the fruits gathered from these for the profit of spiritual life; and the rest of the things joined to them in fair patterns, only to change and begin again with things that are inferior to these. That, I think, is not the act of a man who discerns well. For a mere name brings no profit to some. Therefore it is good that each one remain in the calling in which he was called, being zealous now in what pleases our Lord [?]. However, as sharers in your joy, if you seek counsel, I can show you who is fit for the service of your church and the governance of the community, when the Lord wills. For by God's grace there are those who are fit for this, even if they are much despised, and the Lord knows those who are his. In his grace he cares for his church in the fitting state, and he bestows on the whole of us the gift of his help. Be zealous, therefore, my beloved brothers, in the service of your office, and turn the expectation of your hope toward the mercies of God, so that he in his grace may help you in every matter, keep you unharmed, and fill
your lack with the mercies of his goodness. And pray for my lowliness, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God. Ended.

51. To the saints of our Lord and my fathers, Mar Habib, Mar Zozoy, Mar Narsai and Mar Maremmeh, and those with them who wrote to me. The son in the bosom of the love of your paternity, Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord.

I received and read what you wrote to me, and I gave thanks to our Lord for your health. But if I say to you what was said: "I thought that he would surely come out to me, stand and call on the name of the Lord, wave his hand over the place, and the leprosy would be healed," what would you say to me? What his servants said to that man? Or how would you rebuke the smallness of my faith, as you would Naaman's wonder at the prophet? For the kind of help I needed called for searching out thoughts and words, and for a persuasive power like his. If you have needed this, that is, in vain, thanks be to the gift of our Lord. But if, like my bodily thoughts and those of people like me, you have not yet reached the point of perfection, how much less have you foreseen the precise condition of the situations at hand? For it would be decided from afar while we look only at the face of the [?] help of the night. Suddenly, too, there are many who give the counsel you have given, who, when they come to examine these situations, do not persist in giving proof in the matter, saying only that it seems expedient so. That is just what seems so to you as well.

Grant therefore, O blessed ones, either the power of help like Elisha's, or prayer for it as partners in suffering, so that you may withhold the foot of your zeal from troubling my people at close quarters. Set apart and consecrate your intention to the Lord, so that through the readiness of your petition something pleasing to our Lord's will may be arranged in peace for my lowliness. And if you are willing for his goodness's sake, pray also that he may direct my weakness without trouble, without stumbling and without sin, so that for the rest of the life that is kept for my weakness in this world, and in every work, I may always help in something pleasing to his will. Ended.

52. To my father, sweet and honoured, Mar Gabriel, the metropolitan bishop; and to my dear and beloved brother, Mar Hormizd the bishop; and, if he is present with you, to the bishop of Beth Lapat who wrote to me, who is still my honoured brother, Mar Maremmeh. Ishoʿyahb, your brother: peace in our Lord.

When I came upon the fresh seal of what you wrote to me, O blessed men, I was truly astonished at what had happened, and in my fear of the change I could not even set myself to reply. But when I opened and read the address to me, I was led to marvel even more. First at this: how the pious man whom a little while ago I had persuaded to send in my place to the father of all, I now find at the beginning of the letter at the head of the ranks of those urging me. And this while he holds the first rank among you, that is, among men who argue

from my passing away and from my refusal to be persuaded, and from the other feeble habits of my simplicity. Second, why your astonishing choice was relied on: that the man whom you did not even [?] to test, you suddenly, before [?] the gathering of peace, placed at the head of the ranks of the Lord's hosts, and sent further, to the lower borders, as in that assembly called the typonikos [?] of Heraclidon [?]. And third, along with these: by what force of compulsion that humble man was kept from delay, so that without hesitation he went down to such a venture in faithful obedience. While I marvelled greatly at these things, O pious fathers, I was also greatly distressed and troubled. I did not dare to blame, and to praise was hard for me. Still, if you say that word came from my side, and that you were confirmed by my trust to hand it over, why did you not write to me with your heart about him whom you so entrusted? For I had, as I still have now, much that is fitting and not fitting to show you, in that I know more, as I would persuade you. Indeed it is for all to know that both [?] and middle Athor, and these neighbouring peoples, [recognise] the excellence of his gentle conduct; that his pure mind, trained in the study of divine teachings, is praised; that his modest bearing, adorned with orderly humility, is honoured; and that his quietness, sweetness and gentleness of discernment are useful. These things, thanks be to the Lord, he has bestowed on this servant of his whom we have mentioned. But beyond this, with regard to youth and the middle practical class, because such things and the middle practical class, because, so to speak, a man [?] and [?], and all the things that resemble these. And from these, as you have also tested, this man we have mentioned already lacks something,

apart from inexperience, or rather from not having met with such things. Yet if someone says that it suffices for a servant of God to be a servant of God, yes, I say so too. But times also need the things of the times. And if someone tramples on this too with a believing mind, all things are possible for the one who believes, as it is written, since the Lord will be the doer. But you, who have so often been victorious through obedience, ought not to have been harmed even a little by the unyielding nature of your caution, and only so until I came; and how, before you arrived, you prevailed. But it persuaded you to send in my place, and the father came here, your caution [?]. And this because I was prevented from coming by bonds, as it were, of incapacity, as you yourself also know. But you have also forgotten the commandments: not only do you no longer have a father in me, but you too, as I think, have removed yourself from me forever. Not so, O blessed one, not so! Show yourself to me in every way, and then go. And take care not to grow faint in your hope. Do not let grief at what has happened overcome you, and do not be carried off by these troubles of mine into despondency. Rather, be roused by hope in our Lord's help. Set straight the shoulder of your obedience to the sweet yoke of Christ. And now that you have bent down and taken it up, do not be oppressed by its burden. As you have already read, it is sweet and light. It loves to be perfected in the weak, and if it finds beauty of nature, it makes its work all the more beautiful. It is good, then, that since you are fit on both counts to receive it, the vineyard of his church should be tilled through you, as well pleases him. May he take care, by the honour and power of the name, to make you profitable in youth, and may the Lord's sheep be seasoned by the salt of your sweetness. And may

the whole work of your ministry be for the glory of all. May the soul of our father find rest in you, and may he give thanks to our Lord for you. And you, O blessed ones, beloved of my soul, who have reproached me, or rather urged me, about coming: be assured and believe that until now my will prevailed in the resistance, but now the resistance has lessened a little. Yet I cannot well [?] the constraints on my coming there, especially since I have heard that our blessed father is setting his face toward here. If it turns out so, I beg that I may see you together with him. But if it happens otherwise, or rather if the necessities of affairs there draw it into delay, write to me as is fitting, so that when I find an opportunity to come, I may see you soon. And pray for me, that I may be counted worthy of God's mercies and see you in peace. Up to here, from the episcopate. From here onward, from the metropolitanate.
